vce-physics12-temperature-and-the-kineti: physics12a1-tkp-1
A patient has a body temperature of 37 °C. What is this temperature on the kelvin scale?
T(K) = T(°C) + 273 = 37 + 273 = 310 K. Subtracting 273 gives 236 K, which is a common conversion error.
physics12a1-tkp-2
According to the kinetic particle model, the temperature of a substance is a measure of the
total energy stored in all the bonds between its particles
average random kinetic energy of its particles
number of particles in the sample
total internal energy of the sample
Temperature is proportional to the average random (translational) kinetic energy of the particles. Total internal energy also depends on the amount of substance and on potential energy.
physics12a1-tkp-3
A sealed, rigid container of gas is heated. Which statement best explains why the gas pressure increases?
The particles repel each other more strongly
The number of particles in the container increases
The particles become larger and take up more space
The particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often and with greater force
Higher temperature means greater average speed, so collisions with the walls are more frequent and each exerts a greater force. The volume and number of particles are unchanged.
physics12a1-tkp-4
Container X holds 1 kg of water at 20 °C and container Y holds 2 kg of water at 20 °C. Which statement is correct?
Y has a higher temperature than X
X and Y have the same internal energy
X has greater internal energy because its particles move faster
X and Y have the same temperature but Y has greater internal energy
Both samples have the same average particle kinetic energy, so the same temperature. Y contains twice as many particles, so its total internal energy is greater.
physics12a1-tkp-5
The absolute temperature of a sample of helium gas is increased from 300 K to 1200 K. The average translational kinetic energy of the atoms becomes
2 times larger and the average speed 2 times larger
2 times larger and the average speed 4 times larger
4 times larger and the average speed 2 times larger
4 times larger and the average speed 4 times larger
Average kinetic energy is proportional to T, so it increases by 1200/300 = 4. Since KE = ½mv², speed increases by √4 = 2.
physics12a1-tkp-6
Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K. (a) Convert 77 K to °C. (b) Convert 20 °C to K. (c) Calculate the temperature difference between them in kelvin. (3 marks)
physics12a1-tkp-7
Distinguish between the temperature and the internal energy of a body, using the kinetic particle model. Use an example comparing two bodies in your answer. (3 marks)

Temperature is a measure of the average random kinetic energy of the particles; internal energy is the total of the kinetic and potential energies of all the particles; example: a bathtub of water and a cup of water at the same temperature have the same average particle KE but the bathtub has far greater internal energy because it has many more particles.
physics12a1-tkp-8
A rigid sealed can contains air. The can is placed in a hot oven. Use the kinetic particle model to explain why the pressure inside the can increases. (3 marks)

Heating increases the average kinetic energy (and speed) of the air particles; particles collide with the can walls more frequently; each collision exerts a greater force (greater change in momentum); the volume and number of particles are constant so the pressure increases.
physics12a1-tkp-9
What is the freezing point of water, 0 °C, on the kelvin scale?
0 K
T(K) = T(°C) + 273, so 0 °C = 273 K. A value of 0 K is absolute zero, not the freezing point of water.
physics12a1-tkp-10
Absolute zero, 0 K, is closest to which temperature on the Celsius scale?
T(°C) = T(K) − 273 = 0 − 273 = −273 °C. The value −373 °C comes from wrongly subtracting 100 as well.
physics12a1-tkp-11
The temperature of a metal block rises by 25 K. What is the change in its temperature on the Celsius scale?
A kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size, so a change of 25 K is a change of 25 °C. Adding 273 applies only when converting a temperature, not a difference.
physics12a1-tkp-12
Tiny pollen grains suspended in water are observed under a microscope to jiggle in random directions. According to the kinetic particle model, this occurs because the grains are
attracted to the walls of the container
repelled by each other because they carry like charges
pushed by convection currents caused by the microscope lamp
bombarded unevenly by fast-moving, randomly moving water molecules

Water molecules are in constant random motion and their collisions with a grain do not balance exactly at every instant, giving a net random push. This is Brownian motion and is evidence for particle motion.
physics12a1-tkp-13
A sample of hydrogen gas (molecular mass 2 u) and a sample of oxygen gas (molecular mass 32 u) are both at 300 K. Compared with oxygen molecules, the hydrogen molecules have
the same average kinetic energy but a greater average speed
a greater average kinetic energy and a greater average speed
the same average kinetic energy and the same average speed
a smaller average kinetic energy but a greater average speed
At the same temperature the average translational kinetic energy is the same for all gases. Since KE = ½mv², the lighter hydrogen molecules must move faster on average.
physics12a1-tkp-14
In the kinetic particle model, absolute zero is the temperature at which the particles of a substance
are all at rest relative to each other and exert no forces
have the greatest possible potential energy
have the minimum possible random kinetic energy
change from a liquid to a solid

Temperature measures average random kinetic energy, so 0 K corresponds to the lowest possible random kinetic energy, and no lower temperature exists. Melting and freezing occur at different, substance-dependent temperatures.
physics12a1-tkp-15
The temperature of a gas is raised from 27 °C to 327 °C. The average translational kinetic energy of its particles
increases by a factor of about 12
increases by 300 J
remains the same
doubles
In kelvin the temperature rises from 300 K to 600 K, and average kinetic energy is proportional to T in kelvin, so it doubles. Using the Celsius values gives the incorrect factor of about 12.
physics12a1-tkp-16
Two objects are placed in contact and, after some time, there is no net transfer of energy between them. According to the kinetic particle model, the objects now have the same
average random kinetic energy per particle
total internal energy
number of particles
average particle speed, even if the particle masses differ

Thermal equilibrium means equal temperature, which means equal average random kinetic energy per particle. Equal speeds would only follow if the particles had equal mass, and total internal energy depends on the amount of substance.
physics12a1-tkp-17
A large bath of water at 30 °C is in thermal contact with a small cup of water at 80 °C. The net transfer of energy is
from the bath to the cup, because the bath has more internal energy
zero, because both contain the same substance
from the cup to the bath, because the cup has the higher temperature
from the bath to the cup, because the bath has more particles

Net energy transfer is from the higher-temperature body to the lower-temperature body, because particles with greater average kinetic energy lose energy in collisions. The bath's greater total internal energy is irrelevant to the direction.
physics12a1-tkp-18
A gas is trapped in a sealed syringe at constant temperature. The plunger is pushed in so that the volume is halved. The pressure of the gas increases because
the particles move faster
the particles hit the walls more often, since they have less distance to travel between collisions
the particles become heavier
each collision with the wall exerts a greater force
At constant temperature the average speed, and so the force per collision, is unchanged. In a smaller volume the particles strike the walls more frequently, so the pressure rises.
physics12a1-tkp-19
Which of the following is an assumption of the kinetic particle model of an ideal gas?
The particles attract each other strongly at all separations
The particles collide with the walls and each other so that they lose energy each time
The volume of the particles is much greater than the volume of the container
There are negligible forces between the particles except during collisions

An ideal gas has particles that are very small compared with their separation and interact only through brief, elastic collisions. Attractive forces at all separations or energy loss at each collision are not assumed.
physics12a1-tkp-20
A solid block is heated and its temperature rises while it remains solid. Which change best describes the particles?
They vibrate about their fixed positions with a greater average kinetic energy
They begin to move freely throughout the whole block
They become more tightly packed
They break away from the block and move through the air

In a solid the particles are held in fixed positions and vibrate. Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy, and so the vibration, without letting the particles move freely, which would require melting.
physics12a1-tkp-21
A liquid-in-glass thermometer is calibrated by marking the liquid level at two fixed points. On the Celsius scale these fixed points are
−273 °C and 0 °C
0 °C at the freezing point of water and 273 °C at absolute zero
0 °C at the freezing point and 100 °C at the boiling point of water at standard atmospheric pressure
37 °C at body temperature and 100 °C at the boiling point of water

The Celsius scale is defined using the freezing and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure, with equal divisions between. Absolute zero is the basis of the kelvin scale, and body temperature is not a fixed point.
physics12a1-tkp-22
Why does the gas in a sealed container exert the same pressure on every wall, if the container is at a uniform temperature?
Gravity pulls the particles equally in every direction
The particles move randomly in all directions, so on average equal numbers collide with each wall
The particles only move in straight lines between the walls
The walls are made of the same material
Particle motion is random, with no preferred direction, so each wall receives the same average collision rate and force. Gravity has a negligible effect on the particles of a gas.
physics12a1-tkp-23
A sealed sample of gas is at 20 °C. It is heated until the average kinetic energy of its particles has doubled. The final temperature is closest to
1 K

Average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature: 293 K × 2 = 586 K, which is 586 − 273 = 313 °C. Doubling the Celsius value to 40 °C is a common error, and 586 is the kelvin value, not Celsius.
physics12a1-tkp-24
The temperature of a gas rises from 300 K to 900 K. The average speed of its particles increases by a factor of approximately
Kinetic energy is proportional to T, so it rises by 900/300 = 3. Speed is proportional to the square root of that, √3 ≈ 1.7. A factor of 3 applies to the energy, not the speed.
physics12a1-tkp-25
A block of ice at 0 °C is heated and begins to melt. While it is melting, the temperature stays at 0 °C. According to the kinetic particle model, the energy supplied is
converted into an increase in the average kinetic energy of the particles
lost to the surroundings so the particles slow down
used to make the particles more massive
used to increase the potential energy of the particles as the bonds between them are loosened

The temperature, and so the average kinetic energy, is constant during a phase change. The energy supplied raises the potential energy by loosening the arrangement of particles and so increases the internal energy.
physics12a1-tkp-26
(a) Convert 25 °C to kelvin. (b) Convert 350 K to degrees Celsius. (2 marks)
physics12a1-tkp-27
Tiny smoke particles in air are seen under a microscope to move in a random, jerky manner. Explain this observation using the kinetic particle model. (3 marks)

Air molecules are in constant random motion [1]; they collide with the smoke particles from all directions [1]; at any instant the collisions on different sides do not balance, so there is a net force and the smoke particle moves in a random, jerky way [1].
physics12a1-tkp-28

Helium (atomic mass 4 u) and methane (molecular mass 16 u) gases are at the same temperature. Compare their average translational kinetic energies and calculate the ratio of the average speed of helium particles to that of methane particles. (3 marks)

At the same temperature the average translational kinetic energies are equal [1]; since ½mv² is equal, v is proportional to 1/√m [1]; ratio of speeds = √(16/4) = 2, so helium particles are on average twice as fast [1].
physics12a1-tkp-29
Use the kinetic particle model to explain what is meant by two objects in thermal contact reaching thermal equilibrium. (3 marks)

When the objects are in contact, particles at the interface collide and transfer kinetic energy from the particles with greater average kinetic energy to those with less [1]; there is a net transfer from the hotter to the colder object until the average random kinetic energy per particle is the same in both [1]; at this point the temperatures are equal and there is no net energy transfer [1].
physics12a1-tkp-30
Compare the arrangement and motion of particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas. (3 marks)

Solid: particles are closely packed in fixed positions and vibrate about them [1]; liquid: particles are close together but not in fixed positions, and they move past one another [1]; gas: particles are far apart and move rapidly and randomly, with negligible forces between them except in collisions [1].
physics12a1-tkp-31
A sample of gas is cooled from 120 °C to −153 °C. (a) Express both temperatures in kelvin. (b) Calculate the change in temperature in kelvin. (3 marks)
physics12a1-tkp-32
When a hot cup of water cools by evaporation, the temperature of the water that remains falls. Use the kinetic particle model to explain why. (3 marks)

The particles in the liquid have a range of kinetic energies, and the fastest, most energetic particles near the surface escape as vapour [1]; the particles that escape take away more than the average kinetic energy [1]; the average kinetic energy of the remaining particles therefore falls, so the temperature decreases [1].
physics12a1-tkp-33
A student states that raising the temperature of a gas from 10 °C to 20 °C doubles the average kinetic energy of its particles. Evaluate this claim with a calculation. (3 marks)

Average kinetic energy is proportional to the temperature in kelvin, not degrees Celsius [1]; 10 °C = 283 K and 20 °C = 293 K [1]; the ratio is 293/283 ≈ 1.04, so the kinetic energy increases by only about 4% and the claim is incorrect [1].
vce-physics12-tk-c1
A gas is heated from 27 °C to 327 °C. The average kinetic energy of its particles:
Increases about twelvefold
Doubles
Stays the same
Increases by 300 J
Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature: 300 K → 600 K is a doubling. Using °C gives the wrong ratio.
vce-physics12-specific-heat-capacity: physics12a1-shc-1
How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 0.500 kg of water from 20 °C to 60 °C? (c of water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Q = mcΔT = 0.500 × 4180 × 40 = 83 600 J = 8.36 × 10⁴ J. Using the final temperature (60) instead of ΔT gives 1.25 × 10⁵ J.
physics12a1-shc-2
Equal masses of metal X (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) and metal Y (c = 380 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) absorb the same amount of energy. Which statement is correct?
Neither temperature changes
X undergoes the greater temperature rise
Y undergoes the greater temperature rise
Both undergo the same temperature rise
ΔT = Q/(mc). With Q and m equal, the metal with the smaller c (Y) has the greater temperature rise.
physics12a1-shc-3
The specific heat capacity of ice is 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. This means that
2100 J is needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of ice by 1 K
1 kg of ice at 0 °C contains 2100 J of energy
ice must be at 2100 K to melt
2100 J is needed to melt 1 kg of ice
Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 K. Melting involves latent heat, not specific heat capacity.
physics12a1-shc-4
A 1500 W immersion heater, with no energy losses, heats 2.0 kg of water for 100 s. The temperature rise of the water is closest to (c of water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Q = Pt = 1500 × 100 = 1.5 × 10⁵ J. ΔT = Q/(mc) = 150 000/(2.0 × 4180) = 17.9 K ≈ 18 K. Forgetting the mass gives 36 K.
physics12a1-shc-5
Coastal cities usually have a smaller daily temperature range than inland cities. This is mainly because water
has a high specific heat capacity, so its temperature changes little for a large energy change
has a low specific heat capacity, so it heats up quickly
is a good conductor of heat
reflects all incoming radiation
Water's high specific heat capacity means large amounts of energy are absorbed or released for small temperature changes, moderating the temperature of nearby land.
physics12a1-shc-6

A 0.250 kg aluminium block at 100.0 °C is placed in 0.400 kg of water at 20.0 °C in an insulated container. Calculate the final equilibrium temperature. Use c(aluminium) = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and c(water) = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. (4 marks)
physics12a1-shc-7

A 2000 W electric kettle heats 1.50 kg of water from 18.0 °C to 100 °C. (a) Calculate the energy absorbed by the water. (b) Calculate the time taken if the kettle is 100% efficient. (c) Calculate the time taken if only 85% of the electrical energy is transferred to the water. (4 marks)
physics12a1-shc-8

In an experiment, a 50 W heater is placed in a 1.0 kg metal block for 300 s and the block temperature rises by 17 K. (a) Calculate the value of the specific heat capacity of the metal that a student would obtain from these data. (b) The true value is lower than the student's value. Explain why, and suggest one improvement. (3 marks)

(a) Q = Pt = 50 × 300 = 15 000 J; c = Q/(mΔT) = 15 000/(1.0 × 17) = 882 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (≈ 880); (b) some energy is lost to the surroundings so the block gains less energy than Pt, yet the student used the full Pt, giving too large a value; improvement: insulate the block (e.g. lag it with foam).
physics12a1-shc-9
Which of the following is the SI unit of specific heat capacity?
J K⁻¹
J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
J kg K⁻¹
kg J⁻¹ K
Specific heat capacity is energy per unit mass per unit temperature change, so its unit is J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. J K⁻¹ is the unit of heat capacity of a whole object, which does not include the mass.
physics12a1-shc-10
How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 2.0 kg of copper from 25 °C to 75 °C? (c of copper = 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Q = mcΔT = 2.0 × 385 × 50 = 38 500 J = 3.85 × 10⁴ J. Leaving out the mass gives 1.93 × 10⁴ J.
physics12a1-shc-11
An oil of specific heat capacity 2000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ absorbs 3.0 × 10⁴ J. If the mass of oil is 0.50 kg, its temperature rise is
ΔT = Q/(mc) = 30 000/(0.50 × 2000) = 30 K. Forgetting the mass gives 15 K.
physics12a1-shc-12
A graph of energy supplied Q (vertical axis) against temperature change ΔT (horizontal axis) is plotted for a sample of a substance. The gradient of the line equals
mc, the mass multiplied by the specific heat capacity
c/m
m/c
Q = mcΔT, so Q plotted against ΔT is a straight line with gradient mc. The gradient 1/(mc) would apply if ΔT were plotted against Q.
physics12a1-shc-13
2.0 kg of water at 30 °C is mixed with 1.0 kg of water at 60 °C in an insulated container. The final temperature is
Energy lost = energy gained: 1.0 × (60 − T) = 2.0 × (T − 30), so 120 = 3T and T = 40 °C. The simple average of 45 °C ignores that there is twice as much cooler water.
physics12a1-shc-14
1.0 kg of water and 1.0 kg of copper are each heated through 10 K. Which statement is correct?
The copper requires more energy because it conducts heat better
The water requires less energy because it is a liquid
The water requires more energy because it has the greater specific heat capacity
Both require the same energy because the masses and temperature changes are equal
Q = mcΔT, and with m and ΔT equal the energy depends on c. Water (4180) has a much higher c than copper (385), so it needs more energy.
physics12a1-shc-15
0.20 kg of copper cools from 150 °C to 50 °C. The energy released is (c of copper = 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Q = mcΔT = 0.20 × 385 × 100 = 7700 J. Using the final temperature gives 3.85 × 10³ J, and using the initial temperature gives 1.16 × 10⁴ J; neither is the temperature change.
physics12a1-shc-16
Water is commonly used as the coolant in car engines mainly because it
can absorb a large amount of energy for each kelvin of temperature rise
has a very low boiling point
has a lower specific heat capacity than metals
does not expand when heated
Water's high specific heat capacity lets it carry away a lot of energy per kilogram with only a small temperature rise. A low specific heat capacity would make it a poor coolant.
physics12a1-shc-17
Two samples of equal mass are heated by identical heaters and their temperatures are recorded against time. Sample P warms more quickly than sample Q. This shows that
P has a higher specific heat capacity than Q
P has a lower specific heat capacity than Q
P and Q have the same specific heat capacity
P has a higher melting point than Q
With the same energy supplied each second and equal masses, ΔT = Q/(mc) is larger for the substance with the smaller c. A higher c would give a slower rise.
physics12a1-shc-18
A 0.50 kg metal sample absorbs 9.0 × 10³ J and its temperature rises by 40 K. Its specific heat capacity is
225 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
c = Q/(mΔT) = 9000/(0.50 × 40) = 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Leaving out the mass gives 225 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
physics12a1-shc-19
In an experiment to find the specific heat capacity of a liquid heated by an electric heater, the liquid is stirred continuously. The main reason is to
make the temperature uniform so the thermometer reading represents the whole liquid
increase the specific heat capacity of the liquid
reduce the mass of liquid being heated
remove the need to measure the heating time
Stirring spreads the energy so the whole liquid is at the same temperature as the thermometer. It does not change c, and the time is still needed to find Q = Pt.
physics12a1-shc-20
1.0 kg of water at 20 °C and 1.0 kg of aluminium at 100 °C are placed in contact in an insulated container. The final temperature will be
exactly 60 °C, because the masses are equal
closer to 20 °C than to 100 °C, because water has the greater specific heat capacity
closer to 100 °C than to 20 °C, because aluminium is hotter
closer to 20 °C than to 100 °C, because water has the lower specific heat capacity
Equal masses but c(water) is about 4.6 times c(aluminium), so the water's temperature changes less. The average of 60 °C would apply only if the specific heat capacities were equal.
physics12a1-shc-21
On a sunny day the sand on a beach becomes much hotter than the sea beside it. The best explanation is that sand
has a higher specific heat capacity than water
absorbs more solar energy than water in every case
cannot lose energy to the air
has a lower specific heat capacity than water, so the same energy produces a larger temperature rise
For similar absorbed energy per kilogram, ΔT = Q/(mc) is larger for sand because its c is much smaller than that of water. A higher c would make the sand cooler, not hotter.
physics12a1-shc-22
Samples A and B are both made of the same metal. A has mass 1.0 kg and B has mass 2.0 kg. The same amount of energy is supplied to each. The ratio ΔT(A) : ΔT(B) is
With c and Q equal, ΔT = Q/(mc) is inversely proportional to mass, so the lighter sample A warms twice as much. 1 : 2 reverses the ratio.
physics12a1-shc-23
A 2400 W heater transfers 90% of its electrical energy to 1.0 kg of water for 60 s. The temperature rise of the water is closest to (c of water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Useful energy = 0.90 × 2400 × 60 = 1.296 × 10⁵ J, so ΔT = 129 600/4180 = 31 K. Assuming 100% efficiency gives 34 K.
physics12a1-shc-24
The temperature of a block rises by 35 °C. This is a temperature change of
A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K, so ΔT is the same number in either unit. Adding 273 applies to converting temperatures, not temperature changes.
physics12a1-shc-25
The specific heat capacity of water can be written as 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. The energy needed to raise 200 g of water by 10 K is
Q = mcΔT = 200 × 4.18 × 10 = 8360 J. Using 200 g with 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ without converting to kg gives 8.36 × 10⁶ J.
physics12a1-shc-26
Define specific heat capacity and state its SI unit. (2 marks)
Specific heat capacity is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K [1]; its SI unit is J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ [1].
physics12a1-shc-27

An electric heater of power 2400 W, which transfers all its energy to the water, is used to heat 5.0 kg of water at 15 °C for 4.0 minutes. Calculate the final temperature of the water. (c of water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) (3 marks)
physics12a1-shc-28
Describe an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block using an electric heater. Include the measurements made and how the result is calculated. (4 marks)

Measure the mass of the block with a balance [1]; heat it with an electric heater of known power (or measured voltage and current) for a measured time, recording the initial and final temperatures with a thermometer, with the block insulated to reduce losses [1]; calculate the energy supplied using Q = Pt (or VIt) and the temperature rise ΔT [1]; calculate c = Q/(mΔT) [1].
physics12a1-shc-29

A 0.300 kg metal sample at 100.0 °C is placed in 0.200 kg of water at 20.0 °C in an insulated container. The final temperature is 26.0 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal. (c of water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) (4 marks)
physics12a1-shc-30
A 500 W heater, with no energy losses, is used to raise the temperature of a 0.80 kg aluminium block by 45 K. Calculate the time the heater must be on. (c of aluminium = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) (3 marks)
vce-physics12-sh-c1
200 g of water at 80 °C is mixed with 300 g of water at 20 °C. Ignoring losses, the final temperature is:
Heat lost = heat gained: 0.200 × c × (80 − T) = 0.300 × c × (T − 20), so T = (200 × 80 + 300 × 20) ÷ 500 = 44 °C. It is closer to 20 °C because there is more cold water.
vce-physics12-latent-heat-and-phase-chan: physics12a1-lat-1
How much energy is needed to melt 0.200 kg of ice at 0 °C? (latent heat of fusion of water = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)
Q = mL = 0.200 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 6.68 × 10⁴ J. Using the latent heat of vaporisation would give 4.52 × 10⁵ J.
physics12a1-lat-2
Water is boiling at a steady 100 °C on a stove. According to the kinetic particle model, the energy supplied is being used to
reduce the mass of the water
increase the average kinetic energy of the particles
increase the potential energy of the particles as the bonds between them are overcome
decrease the number of particles
During a phase change, temperature (average KE) is constant; the energy increases the potential energy of the particles as intermolecular bonds are broken.
physics12a1-lat-3
Steam at 100 °C causes a more severe burn than the same mass of water at 100 °C because
steam releases a large amount of latent heat as it condenses on the skin
steam has a lower specific heat capacity than water
steam conducts heat better than water
steam has a higher temperature
Condensation releases 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ before the condensed water cools further, so much more energy is transferred to the skin.
physics12a1-lat-4

1 kg of ice at −10 °C is heated at a constant rate until it is steam at 110 °C. Which stage of the process takes the longest time? (c ice = 2100, c water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; L fusion = 3.34 × 10⁵, L vaporisation = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)
warming the water from 0 °C to 100 °C
boiling the water to steam
warming the ice to 0 °C
melting the ice
The energies are about 2.1 × 10⁴ J, 3.34 × 10⁵ J, 4.18 × 10⁵ J and 2.26 × 10⁶ J respectively. At a constant power the largest energy takes the longest time: vaporisation.
physics12a1-lat-5
How much energy is required to change 0.100 kg of ice at 0 °C to water at 20 °C? (L fusion = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; c water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
physics12a1-lat-6

Calculate the energy required to change 0.300 kg of ice at −10.0 °C into steam at 100 °C. Data: c ice = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; c water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; L fusion = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; L vaporisation = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. (4 marks)
physics12a1-lat-7

A 0.0500 kg piece of ice at 0 °C is placed in 0.300 kg of water at 25.0 °C in an insulated container. Calculate the final temperature, assuming all the ice melts and no energy is lost. (L fusion = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; c water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) (4 marks)
physics12a1-lat-8
A block of ice at 0 °C is heated steadily. Using the kinetic particle model, explain why its temperature stays constant while it melts even though energy is being supplied. (3 marks)

Temperature depends on average kinetic energy of the particles; during melting the supplied energy is used to break the bonds holding particles in a fixed lattice, increasing their potential energy; the kinetic energy (and so temperature) does not change until all the ice has melted.
physics12a1-lat-9
What is meant by the specific latent heat of fusion of a substance?
The energy needed to melt 1 kg of the solid at its melting point without a change in temperature
The energy needed to raise 1 kg of the solid by 1 K
The energy needed to turn 1 kg of liquid into gas at its boiling point
The energy released when 1 kg of liquid cools by 1 K
It is the energy per kilogram to change solid to liquid at constant temperature. Raising the temperature by 1 K describes specific heat capacity, not latent heat.
physics12a1-lat-10
Which is the correct SI unit for specific latent heat?
J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
J kg⁻¹
J K⁻¹
J kg
Q = mL, so L = Q/m has units J kg⁻¹. The unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ belongs to specific heat capacity, which involves a temperature change.
physics12a1-lat-11
Calculate the energy needed to vaporise 0.500 kg of water at 100 °C. (L vaporisation = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)
Q = mL = 0.500 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 1.13 × 10⁶ J. Forgetting to multiply by the mass gives 2.26 × 10⁶ J.
physics12a1-lat-12
What mass of ice at 0 °C can be melted by 1.67 × 10⁵ J of energy? (L fusion = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)
m = Q/L = 1.67 × 10⁵ ÷ 3.34 × 10⁵ = 0.500 kg. Inverting the ratio gives 2.00 kg.
physics12a1-lat-13
On a graph of temperature against energy supplied for a substance heated at a constant rate, the horizontal sections represent
changes of state, where energy goes into potential energy and temperature is constant
the substance not absorbing any energy
the specific heat capacity becoming zero because the substance is insulated
the particles stopping moving
Flat sections are phase changes: energy is absorbed but used to change particle separation (potential energy), so the temperature does not change. Energy is still being absorbed.
physics12a1-lat-14
The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is much greater than its specific latent heat of fusion. The best explanation is that
water particles are heavier in the gas phase
vaporisation completely separates the particles and also does work pushing back the atmosphere
water boils at a higher temperature than it melts, so the particles move faster
ice has already lost most of its bonds before it melts

Turning liquid into gas removes almost all intermolecular attraction and requires expansion against the atmosphere, whereas melting only loosens the bonds. Higher temperature is not the reason, because the average kinetic energy does not change during the phase change.
physics12a1-lat-15
How much energy is released when 0.250 kg of water at 0 °C freezes to ice at 0 °C? (L fusion = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)
Q = mL = 0.250 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 8.35 × 10⁴ J released. Using 4180 × 100 would wrongly include cooling to 0 °C, which has already happened.
physics12a1-lat-16
Evaporation of sweat cools the skin. According to the particle model, this is because
the sweat particles gain energy from the air and become colder
evaporation increases the mass of the sweat
evaporating particles stop moving
the most energetic particles escape the liquid, lowering the average kinetic energy of those left

Only the fastest particles have enough energy to escape, so the average kinetic energy (and temperature) of the remaining liquid falls. Escaping particles do not become colder by gaining energy; they carry energy away.
physics12a1-lat-17
A 500 W heater supplies all its energy to 0.100 kg of ice at 0 °C. How long does it take to melt all the ice? (L fusion = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)
Energy = 0.100 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 3.34 × 10⁴ J. Time = E/P = 33 400 ÷ 500 = 66.8 s. Using the mass 1 kg would give 668 s.
physics12a1-lat-18
How much energy is released when 0.0200 kg of steam at 100 °C condenses to water at 100 °C? (L vaporisation = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)
Q = mL = 0.0200 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 4.52 × 10⁴ J. The question stops at water at 100 °C, so no cooling energy should be added.
physics12a1-lat-19
As liquid water at 0 °C freezes to ice at 0 °C, the internal energy of the water
stays the same because the temperature is constant
decreases because the kinetic energy of the particles decreases
decreases because the potential energy of the particles decreases
increases because the particles become more ordered
Freezing releases latent heat, so internal energy falls. Since the temperature is constant the kinetic energy is unchanged; it is the potential energy that decreases as bonds form.
physics12a1-lat-20
A substance is heated by a constant power supply, and its temperature is plotted against time. The solid section of the graph is steeper than the liquid section. This is because the solid has
a higher specific heat capacity than the liquid
a lower latent heat than the liquid
a higher mass than the liquid
a lower specific heat capacity than the liquid
With constant power, ΔT/time = P/(mc). A steeper slope means a smaller c. Mass is the same in both sections, and latent heat only affects the flat sections.
physics12a1-lat-21
Sublimation is the process in which a substance
changes from gas to liquid
changes directly from solid to gas without becoming liquid
melts and then immediately boils
changes from liquid to solid
Sublimation is solid to gas directly, as for dry ice (solid CO₂) at atmospheric pressure. Gas to liquid is condensation.
physics12a1-lat-22
Ice cubes at 0 °C cool a drink more effectively than the same mass of water at 0 °C because the ice
has a higher specific heat capacity
is a lower temperature
absorbs a large amount of latent heat as it melts
has more particles

Melting absorbs 3.34 × 10⁵ J per kg from the drink with no temperature rise, in addition to the energy absorbed warming the melt water. Both samples are at 0 °C and the same mass has the same number of particles.
physics12a1-lat-23
What mass of steam at 100 °C must condense to water at 100 °C to release 1.13 × 10⁵ J? (L vaporisation = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)
m = Q/L = 1.13 × 10⁵ ÷ 2.26 × 10⁶ = 0.0500 kg. Using the latent heat of fusion would give 0.338 kg.
physics12a1-lat-24
Calculate the energy released when 0.100 kg of steam at 100 °C is converted to water at 50.0 °C. (L vaporisation = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; c water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Condensing: 0.100 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 226 000 J. Cooling: 0.100 × 4180 × 50.0 = 20 900 J. Total = 246 900 J ≈ 2.47 × 10⁵ J. Counting only condensation gives 2.26 × 10⁵ J.
physics12a1-lat-25
Define the specific latent heat of vaporisation of a substance and state its SI unit. (2 marks)
Specific latent heat of vaporisation is the energy required to change 1 kg of a liquid to a gas at its boiling point without a change in temperature [1]; unit J kg⁻¹ [1].
physics12a1-lat-26

Steam of mass 0.0400 kg at 100 °C is bubbled into 0.500 kg of water at 20.0 °C in an insulated container. Assuming all the steam condenses and no energy is lost, calculate the final temperature of the water. (L vaporisation = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; c water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) (4 marks)

Energy released by condensing = 0.0400 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 90 400 J [1]; energy released by condensed water cooling = 0.0400 × 4180 × (100 − T) [1]; energy gained by cool water = 0.500 × 4180 × (T − 20.0) [1]; equate: 90 400 + 167.2(100 − T) = 2090(T − 20.0), giving T = 66.0 °C [1].
physics12a1-lat-27
A sample of ice at −20 °C is heated at a constant rate until it becomes steam above 100 °C. Describe the shape of the graph of temperature against time. (4 marks)

Temperature rises steadily as ice warms to 0 °C [1]; a horizontal section at 0 °C while the ice melts [1]; a rise to 100 °C that is less steep than the ice section, as water has a higher specific heat capacity [1]; a longer horizontal section at 100 °C during boiling because L vaporisation is much greater than L fusion, then a steady rise as steam is heated [1].
physics12a1-lat-28

Ice at 0 °C is added to 0.250 kg of water at 30.0 °C to cool it to 0 °C. Calculate the mass of ice that must melt. Assume no energy is lost to the surroundings. (L fusion = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; c water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) (3 marks)
Energy released by water cooling = 0.250 × 4180 × 30.0 = 31 350 J [1]; energy absorbed by melting ice = mL, so 31 350 = m × 3.34 × 10⁵ [1]; m = 0.0939 kg [1].
physics12a1-lat-29

A freezer removes energy at a constant rate of 150 W from 0.400 kg of water at 20.0 °C. Calculate the time taken for the water to cool and freeze completely to ice at 0 °C. (L fusion = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; c water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) (3 marks)
physics12a1-lat-30

A 0.100 kg block of ice at −20.0 °C is placed in 0.400 kg of water at 40.0 °C in an insulated container. Calculate the final temperature, assuming no energy is lost. (c ice = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; c water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; L fusion = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹) (4 marks)

Energy to warm ice to 0 °C = 0.100 × 2100 × 20.0 = 4200 J; energy to melt = 0.100 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 33 400 J; total 37 600 J, less than the 66 880 J available from cooling the water to 0 °C so all the ice melts [1]; energy to warm melted ice: 0.100 × 4180 × T = 418T [1]; energy released by warm water: 0.400 × 4180 × (40.0 − T) = 1672(40.0 − T) [1]; 37 600 + 418T = 66 880 − 1672T, giving T = 14.0 °C [1].
vce-physics12-lh-c1
How much energy is needed to turn 0.50 kg of ice at −10 °C into water at 20 °C?
About 2.2 × 10⁵ J
Warm the ice: 0.50 × 2100 × 10 = 10 500 J. Melt it: 0.50 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 167 000 J. Warm the water: 0.50 × 4200 × 20 = 42 000 J. Total ≈ 219 500 J. Melting needs by far the most energy.
vce-physics12-conduction-convection-and-: physics12a1-ccr-1
Which method of thermal energy transfer can occur across a vacuum?
convection
radiation
conduction and convection
conduction
Radiation is transferred by electromagnetic waves and requires no medium. Conduction and convection need particles.
physics12a1-ccr-2
Metals are good thermal conductors mainly because
they have a high specific heat capacity
their particles are closely packed and large
they contain delocalised electrons that transfer energy quickly
they are always at a higher temperature than non-metals
Free (delocalised) electrons move rapidly through the metal and transfer kinetic energy, in addition to lattice vibrations being passed on.
physics12a1-ccr-3
On a sunny afternoon at the beach, a breeze blows from the sea towards the land. This is best explained by
warm air over the land rising and cooler, denser air from the sea moving in to replace it
radiation from the sea heating the land
the sea having a lower specific heat capacity than land
conduction of heat from the sand to the sea
Land heats faster than water, warming the air above it. This air expands, becomes less dense and rises (convection), and cooler air from the sea flows in.
physics12a1-ccr-4

A wall of thickness 0.10 m conducts energy at a rate of 40 W for a given temperature difference. The wall is replaced by the same material of thickness 0.20 m with the same area and the same temperature difference. The rate of conduction becomes
Conduction rate is inversely proportional to thickness for a given area and temperature difference. Doubling the thickness halves the rate: 20 W.
physics12a1-ccr-5
Double-glazed windows reduce heat loss mainly because
glass reflects all infrared radiation
the trapped layer of air or vacuum between the panes is a poor conductor and limits convection
glass is a perfect insulator
the second pane increases the temperature of the room
A thin trapped air (or evacuated) layer has low thermal conductivity and is too thin for significant convection currents, so conduction and convection losses are reduced.
physics12a1-ccr-6
A ceramic tile and a woollen carpet are both at room temperature (20 °C), yet the tile feels much colder to bare feet. Explain why. (3 marks)

The tile is a better thermal conductor than the carpet; energy is conducted from the warmer foot to the tile at a faster rate; skin temperature drops more quickly (and the carpet, a poor conductor, stays warm at the surface), so the tile feels colder even though both are at the same temperature.
physics12a1-ccr-7
A pot of water is heated on an electric stove element. Describe how energy is transferred from the element to the water at the top of the pot. (3 marks)

Energy is conducted from the element through the base of the pot to the water at the bottom; the heated water expands, becomes less dense and rises while cooler, denser water sinks, forming convection currents; this circulation transports energy throughout the water to the top.
physics12a1-ccr-8

A vacuum flask has a double-walled glass container with the space between the walls evacuated and the inner surfaces silvered, plus an insulating stopper. Identify the main mode of energy transfer that each feature reduces. (3 marks)

Evacuated space between the walls reduces conduction and convection (no particles to transfer energy); silvered surfaces reduce radiation (low emissivity, reflecting infrared); insulating stopper reduces conduction and convection at the opening (poor conductor and traps air).
physics12a1-ccr-9
Convection can occur only in
solids and liquids
solids only
fluids (liquids and gases)
a vacuum
Convection relies on bulk movement of a fluid, which can flow and form currents. Solids cannot circulate in this way, and a vacuum has no particles to move.
physics12a1-ccr-10
In a non-metal solid such as wood or glass, energy is conducted mainly by
vibrations passed between neighbouring particles
delocalised electrons moving through the solid
bulk movement of heated material
electromagnetic waves travelling through the solid
Non-metals have no free electrons, so energy passes from particle to particle as vibrations. Delocalised electrons are the extra mechanism in metals only.
physics12a1-ccr-11
Which surface is the best absorber of thermal radiation?
white and glossy
polished silver
shiny aluminium foil
matt black
Dark, matt surfaces absorb most of the radiation that falls on them. Light, shiny surfaces reflect much of it.
physics12a1-ccr-12
A slab conducts energy at 30 W. The area is doubled while the thickness and the temperature difference stay the same. The rate of conduction becomes
Rate of conduction is directly proportional to area, so doubling the area doubles the rate to 60 W. It is the thickness, not the area, that has an inverse relationship.
physics12a1-ccr-13
A slab conducts energy at 25 W when the temperature difference across it is 10 K. If the temperature difference is increased to 20 K, with everything else unchanged, the rate becomes
Rate of conduction is directly proportional to temperature difference, so doubling it doubles the rate to 50 W. Squaring the change (100 W) would be wrong because the relationship is linear.
physics12a1-ccr-14
The rate of conduction is given by P = kAΔT/L. A glass pane has k = 0.80 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, area 2.0 m², thickness 0.010 m and a temperature difference of 5.0 K across it. The rate of energy transfer is
P = 0.80 × 2.0 × 5.0 ÷ 0.010 = 800 W. Multiplying by the thickness instead of dividing gives the incorrect 0.080 W.
physics12a1-ccr-15
A hot air balloon rises when its burner heats the air inside the envelope. This is because the heated air
has more mass than the surrounding air
radiates energy upwards
has a greater specific heat capacity
expands and becomes less dense than the surrounding air
Heated air expands, so its density falls below that of the cooler air outside and it is pushed upwards. Heating does not increase the mass of air in the balloon.
physics12a1-ccr-16
The heating element of an electric kettle is placed at the base because
hot water sinks and carries energy to the cooler water above
heated water at the base rises while cooler water sinks, setting up convection currents
water is a good conductor so energy passes quickly upwards
the base radiates energy mainly upwards through the lid
Water at the base expands, becomes less dense and rises, while denser cool water sinks to replace it. Hot water does not sink, which makes the first option wrong.
physics12a1-ccr-17
A split-system air conditioner used for cooling is mounted high on a wall. This is effective because
cool air is less dense and rises to fill the room
warm air at floor level is conducted to the unit
cool air from the unit is denser and sinks, so warmer air rises and is drawn in to be cooled
radiation from the unit travels horizontally across the room
Cooled air is denser and sinks, pushing warmer air up towards the unit and creating a convection current. Cool air does not rise, so the first option has the density relationship reversed.
physics12a1-ccr-18
The SI unit of thermal conductivity, k, is
W m⁻¹ K⁻¹
J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
W m⁻² K
J m⁻¹ K⁻¹
From P = kAΔT/L, k = PL/(AΔT), which has units W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the unit of specific heat capacity.
physics12a1-ccr-19
Which of the following is an example of energy transfer mainly by convection?
warmth felt on the face from the Sun
a metal spoon warming in hot tea
heat felt at the hand held beside a lamp
hot air rising from a bitumen road on a summer day
Air heated by the road expands and rises, carrying energy upwards as a convection current. Warmth from the Sun or a lamp is mainly radiation, and the spoon warms by conduction.
physics12a1-ccr-20
Fibreglass batts in a ceiling are effective insulators mainly because
fibreglass is a perfect insulator
they trap many small pockets of air, which conducts poorly and cannot circulate easily
they reflect all convection currents back into the room
glass fibres absorb all the energy that reaches them
The fibres hold air in tiny pockets that limit both conduction (air is a poor conductor) and convection. No material is a perfect insulator.
physics12a1-ccr-21
Which statement about thermal radiation from the Sun is correct?
It is carried by particles in the upper atmosphere
It travels more slowly than visible light
It travels through space as electromagnetic waves at the speed of light
It reaches Earth only by convection currents in space
Thermal radiation is electromagnetic radiation, so it needs no medium and moves at 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum. Space has no particles to support convection.
physics12a1-ccr-22
An object stays at a constant temperature in surroundings at the same temperature. For this object, thermal radiation is
absorbed at the same rate as it is emitted
emitted but not absorbed
absorbed but not emitted
neither emitted nor absorbed
All objects above absolute zero both emit and absorb radiation continuously. A steady temperature means the two rates are equal, not that either has stopped.
physics12a1-ccr-23
As the temperature of a hot object increases, the rate at which it emits thermal radiation
decreases
stays the same
increases only if its surface is shiny
increases
Hotter objects emit radiation at a greater rate regardless of surface type. A shiny surface lowers the amount emitted at any temperature but does not reverse the trend.
physics12a1-ccr-24
A metal rod and a wooden rod of the same size are each heated at one end. The far end of the metal rod becomes warm much sooner because
wood has a higher thermal conductivity
metal has a higher thermal conductivity
the metal rod is always at a higher temperature than the wooden rod
wood transfers energy mainly by radiation
Metal conducts energy far more quickly than wood, so energy reaches the far end sooner. Both rods start at the same temperature, so the difference is not due to initial temperature.
physics12a1-ccr-25
A shiny metallised emergency blanket is wrapped around a person suffering from cold exposure mainly to
reflect infrared radiation from the body back towards the person
increase conduction from the body to the air
absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the body
allow convection currents to carry energy away
The reflective surface has low emissivity and sends the body's radiated energy back, reducing loss. Absorbing it would simply warm the blanket's outer surface and lose energy to the air.
physics12a1-ccr-26

A copper rod conducts 12 W between its ends for a given temperature difference. A second rod of the same copper has half the length and twice the cross-sectional area, with the same temperature difference. It conducts at
Rate is proportional to area and inversely proportional to length, so the factor is 2 × 2 = 4, giving 48 W. Applying only one of the changes gives 24 W.
physics12a1-ccr-27
At night a breeze commonly blows from the land towards the sea because
the land retains energy longer than the sea, so air over the land rises
the land cools faster than the sea, so warmer air over the sea rises and cooler air from the land replaces it
the sea cools faster than the land, so cool sea air is drawn inland
radiation from the land pushes air seawards
Water cools more slowly than land, so air over the sea stays warmer and rises, and cooler air flows in from the land. The reverse of the daytime sea breeze occurs at night.
physics12a1-ccr-28
Radiators in a house are often placed low on a wall, near the floor. Explain how this helps heat the whole room. (2 marks)

Air next to the radiator is heated, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises [1]; cooler, denser air moves in to replace it, producing a convection current that circulates warm air around the room [1].
physics12a1-ccr-29

Insulation in a ceiling is made of material with thermal conductivity 0.040 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. The ceiling has an area of 12 m² and the insulation is 0.10 m thick. Calculate the rate of conduction through the ceiling when the temperature difference across it is 15 K. Use P = kAΔT/L. (3 marks)
Substitute into P = kAΔT/L [1]; P = 0.040 × 12 × 15 ÷ 0.10 [1]; P = 72 W [1].
physics12a1-ccr-30
Two identical cars are parked in the sun. One is painted matt black and the other is painted white. After an hour the black car is much hotter. Explain why. (2 marks)

The matt black surface is a good absorber of radiation, so it absorbs most of the radiation from the Sun [1]; the white surface reflects much of the incident radiation, so less energy is absorbed and the white car warms less [1].
physics12a1-ccr-31
A down jacket is filled with fluffy feathers. Explain why it keeps the wearer warm. (3 marks)

The feathers trap many small pockets of air [1]; air is a poor conductor, so conduction of energy away from the body is reduced [1]; the pockets are too small for convection currents to form, so the trapped air stays still and convection loss is also reduced [1].
physics12a1-ccr-32
Distinguish between conduction and convection as methods of energy transfer. (2 marks)

Conduction transfers energy through a material by collisions or vibrations between neighbouring particles, with no overall movement of the material [1]; convection transfers energy by the bulk movement of a fluid, with heated, less dense fluid rising and cooler fluid sinking [1].
physics12a1-ccr-33

A glass window has thermal conductivity 0.84 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, an area of 1.5 m² and a thickness of 4.0 mm. Calculate the rate of conduction through the window when the temperature difference between its faces is 6.0 K. Use P = kAΔT/L. (3 marks)
physics12a1-ccr-34

A person standing beside a campfire feels warm on the side of their body facing the fire, even though they are not above the flames. Explain why this is mainly due to radiation and not convection or conduction. (2 marks)

Convection currents carry heated air upwards, away from a person standing to the side, and air is a poor conductor [1]; the fire emits infrared radiation in all directions, which travels through the air and is absorbed by the person's skin [1].
physics12a1-ccr-35
The fins on the back of a refrigerator are painted matt black and have a large surface area. Explain how these features help the refrigerator lose energy to the room. (3 marks)

A large surface area increases the area in contact with the air, so more energy is transferred by conduction to the air and convection [1]; matt black surfaces are good emitters of radiation, so more energy is radiated away [1]; warmed air near the fins rises and is replaced by cooler air, which maintains a convection current [1].
physics12a1-ccr-36
A metal spoon left in a bowl of hot soup soon feels hot at the handle, but a wooden spoon does not. Explain this difference. (2 marks)

Metal is a good thermal conductor, so energy is rapidly conducted along the spoon (by free electrons and vibrations) to the handle [1]; wood is a poor conductor, so energy travels along it very slowly and the handle stays cool [1].
vce-physics12-cc-c1
A vacuum flask keeps drinks hot mainly because:
The vacuum stops conduction and convection, and the silvered walls reduce radiation
The vacuum stops radiation only, and the glass walls stop conduction
The glass is a good conductor, so heat spreads evenly and stays in
Convection currents in the vacuum carry heat back into the drink
Conduction and convection need particles; radiation does not, so shiny surfaces are used to reflect it back.
vce-physics12-thermal-radiation-and-wien: physics12a1-wien-1
The surface of the Sun has a temperature of about 5800 K. Using Wien's law with constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K, the peak wavelength of its radiation is closest to
50 nm
500 nm
λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 5800 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm, in the visible region.
physics12a1-wien-2
As the temperature of a hot object (blackbody) increases, which of the following is true?
The peak wavelength and total emitted power both increase
The peak wavelength does not change but total emitted power increases
The peak wavelength increases and total emitted power decreases
The peak wavelength decreases and total emitted power increases
Wien's law: λmax is inversely proportional to T, so peak wavelength shifts to shorter values. Hotter objects also emit more power overall.
physics12a1-wien-3
The human body has a surface temperature of about 310 K. The peak of its thermal radiation lies in the
ultraviolet region
visible region
infrared region
microwave region
λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 310 = 9.35 × 10⁻⁶ m, about 9.4 µm, which is infrared.
physics12a1-wien-4
Star A has a peak emission wavelength of 400 nm and star B has a peak emission wavelength of 800 nm. Assuming both behave as blackbodies, the surface temperature of star A compared with star B is
the same
half as great
twice as great
four times as great
λmax is inversely proportional to T. A has half the peak wavelength, so twice the surface temperature.
physics12a1-wien-5

Two identical cups of hot coffee at 90 °C, one with a matte black surface and one with a shiny silver surface, are left in a room. Which statement is most likely correct about radiation from the cups?
The matte black cup radiates more energy per second
Both radiate the same energy because they are at the same temperature
Neither cup radiates energy
The silver cup radiates more energy per second
Good absorbers are good emitters. A matte black surface has high emissivity and radiates more strongly than shiny silver at the same temperature.
physics12a1-wien-6

The filament of a lamp has a peak emission wavelength of 1.45 µm. (a) Use Wien's law (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K) to calculate the filament temperature. (b) In which region of the electromagnetic spectrum is the peak, and what does this suggest about the efficiency of the lamp for lighting? (3 marks)
(a) T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.00 × 10³ K; (b) peak lies in the infrared; most energy emitted is infrared, not visible, so the lamp is inefficient as a light source.
physics12a1-wien-7
The Earth has an average surface temperature of about 288 K. Calculate the peak wavelength of the radiation it emits and name the region of the spectrum. (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K) (3 marks)
λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 288 (1); = 1.01 × 10⁻⁵ m, or about 10 µm (1); this is in the infrared region (1).
physics12a1-wien-8
Describe how the graph of intensity versus wavelength for a blackbody radiator changes when its temperature is increased. (3 marks)

The graph is a continuous curve with a single peak; as temperature increases the peak moves to a shorter wavelength; the intensity is greater at all wavelengths so the area under the curve (total power emitted) increases.
physics12a1-wien-9
Which statement correctly expresses Wien's law for a blackbody radiator?
The product of the peak wavelength and the absolute temperature is constant
The peak wavelength is directly proportional to the absolute temperature
The peak wavelength is proportional to the square of the absolute temperature
The peak wavelength is independent of the absolute temperature

Wien's law is λmax × T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K, so λmax is inversely proportional to T. A direct proportionality would mean hotter objects peak at longer wavelengths, which is the opposite of what is observed.
physics12a1-wien-10
A tungsten-halogen lamp has a filament at 3000 K. Using Wien's law (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K), its peak wavelength is closest to
97 nm
970 nm
9.7 µm
97 µm
λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 3000 = 9.66 × 10⁻⁷ m, about 970 nm. Options in µm come from dividing incorrectly by a power of ten.
physics12a1-wien-11
A cooling object has its peak thermal emission at a wavelength of 10 µm. Using Wien's law (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K), its temperature is closest to
T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 290 K. Forgetting to convert 10 µm to metres gives an answer out by a power of ten.
physics12a1-wien-12
A metal block is heated from 27 °C to 327 °C. Its peak emission wavelength will
decrease by a factor of about 12
double
stay the same
halve
The temperatures are 300 K and 600 K, so the absolute temperature doubles and the peak wavelength halves. The temperature in °C changes by a factor of 12, but Wien's law must use kelvin.
physics12a1-wien-13
Two stars are observed, one appearing blue and one appearing red. Assuming both behave as blackbodies, which statement is correct?
The blue star is hotter because its peak wavelength is shorter
The red star is hotter because its peak wavelength is longer
The stars have the same temperature but different sizes
The stars must have the same peak wavelength
Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light, and by Wien's law a shorter peak wavelength means a higher temperature. A longer peak wavelength indicates a cooler star.
physics12a1-wien-14
Which statement about thermal radiation is correct?
It is emitted only by objects hotter than 100 °C
It is emitted by all objects with a temperature above absolute zero
It is emitted only by objects that glow visibly
It is emitted only by objects in contact with air
All matter above 0 K emits electromagnetic radiation because of the thermal motion of its charged particles. Most objects at everyday temperatures emit in the infrared, so they do not glow visibly.
physics12a1-wien-15
Energy from the Sun reaches the Earth across the vacuum of space by
conduction through the solar wind
convection currents in space
electromagnetic radiation
sound waves
Radiation is the only form of heat transfer that needs no medium. Conduction and convection both need particles, which are absent in the vacuum of space.
physics12a1-wien-16
An ideal blackbody is best described as an object that
reflects all incident radiation and emits none
emits radiation only in the visible region
is always black in colour at every temperature
absorbs all incident radiation and emits the maximum possible thermal radiation for its temperature
A blackbody is a perfect absorber and therefore also a perfect emitter. It is not necessarily black in colour: the Sun is a close approximation yet appears yellow-white.
physics12a1-wien-17
On a hot sunny day, a person wearing a white shirt tends to feel cooler than a person wearing a black shirt. This is mainly because the white shirt
reflects more of the incident radiation and absorbs less
absorbs more radiation and emits it all away
emits no thermal radiation
is a better conductor of heat
Light, shiny surfaces reflect more incident radiation, so less energy is absorbed. A black shirt absorbs more of the Sun's radiation and warms up faster.
physics12a1-wien-18
The inner walls of a vacuum flask are silvered. This reduces heat transfer mainly because the shiny surface
prevents conduction through the glass
is a poor emitter and a good reflector of thermal radiation
increases convection inside the flask
absorbs radiation and stores it
A silvered surface has low emissivity and reflects radiation back, reducing transfer by radiation. The vacuum between the walls, not the silvering, is what stops conduction and convection.
physics12a1-wien-19
A cup of tea has cooled until its temperature equals that of the surrounding room. Which statement is correct?
The cup has stopped emitting thermal radiation
The cup emits radiation but absorbs none
The cup emits and absorbs radiation at the same rate
The cup absorbs radiation but emits none
In thermal equilibrium the object still emits radiation, but it absorbs radiation from its surroundings at the same rate, so there is no net energy transfer and its temperature stays constant.
physics12a1-wien-20
A hot star has its peak emission at 290 nm. Using Wien's law (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K), its surface temperature is closest to
T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.90 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.0 × 10⁴ K. A 290 nm peak is in the ultraviolet, which indicates a very hot object.
physics12a1-wien-21
Object X is at 300 K and object Y is at 900 K. Both behave as blackbodies. The ratio of the peak wavelength of X to the peak wavelength of Y is
Since λmax is proportional to 1/T, the ratio λX/λY = TY/TX = 900/300 = 3. Inverting this ratio is a common mistake.
physics12a1-wien-22
The element of an electric stove at about 1000 K glows dull red. Using Wien's law (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K), the peak of its emitted radiation is in the
visible region, in the red
infrared region
ultraviolet region
X-ray region
λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 1000 = 2.9 µm, which is infrared. Only the short-wavelength tail of the spectrum reaches the red end of the visible region, which is why the element glows dull red.
physics12a1-wien-23
The cosmic microwave background has a blackbody spectrum corresponding to a temperature of about 2.7 K. Its peak wavelength (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K) is closest to
1.1 µm
11 µm
1.1 mm
11 mm
λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.7 = 1.07 × 10⁻³ m, about 1.1 mm, which is in the microwave region. Very low temperatures give very long peak wavelengths.
physics12a1-wien-24
Solar hot water collector plates are painted matte black because a matte black surface
reflects most of the Sun's radiation
emits no radiation of its own
is a good insulator
is a good absorber of radiation
A matte black surface absorbs a large fraction of the incident radiation, so more of the Sun's energy heats the water. A reflective surface would send much of it away.
physics12a1-wien-25
A pottery kiln wall is at 127 °C. Using Wien's law (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K), the peak wavelength of the radiation it emits is closest to
7.2 µm
23 µm
2.3 µm
T = 127 + 273 = 400 K, so λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 400 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁶ m. Using 127 instead of 400 gives the incorrect 23 µm.
physics12a1-wien-26
On a graph of intensity versus wavelength for a blackbody, the area under the curve represents the
peak wavelength
temperature of the object in kelvin
total power emitted per unit area
range of visible wavelengths emitted
Adding the intensity over all wavelengths gives the total power emitted per unit area. The peak position only tells you the wavelength of greatest intensity, not the total.
physics12a1-wien-27
A star has a peak emission wavelength of 450 nm. Using Wien's law (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K), calculate its surface temperature. (2 marks)
physics12a1-wien-28
A metal sphere is heated from 800 K to 1600 K. State how the peak wavelength of its emitted radiation changes and describe the effect on the proportion of its radiation that is visible. (2 marks)

The peak wavelength halves because it is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature [1]; the peak moves towards the visible region so a greater proportion of the emitted radiation is visible and the sphere glows brighter [1].
physics12a1-wien-29
A furnace operates at 1500 K and a nearby metal bench is at 300 K. Calculate the peak wavelength emitted by each and compare them. (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K) (3 marks)
Furnace: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 1500 = 1.93 × 10⁻⁶ m [1]; bench: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 300 = 9.66 × 10⁻⁶ m [1]; the hotter furnace has a peak wavelength five times shorter than the bench [1].
physics12a1-wien-30
Explain why energy from the Sun can reach the Earth by radiation but not by conduction or convection. (2 marks)

Conduction and convection require a medium (particles) to carry the energy, and space between the Sun and Earth is almost a vacuum [1]; radiation is electromagnetic waves, which can travel through a vacuum without a medium [1].
physics12a1-wien-31

A dark-painted car and a white car are parked in the sun. Explain why the interior of the dark car heats up faster during the day, and why the dark car also loses energy by radiation more quickly at night. (3 marks)

A dark surface is a good absorber so it absorbs more of the Sun's incident radiation than the white surface [1]; good absorbers are also good emitters, so the dark surface has a higher emissivity [1]; therefore at night the dark car radiates more energy per second and cools faster [1].
physics12a1-wien-32
A vacuum flask has double glass walls with the space between them evacuated and the inner surfaces silvered. Explain how these features keep the contents hot. (3 marks)

The vacuum between the walls prevents conduction and convection across the gap [1]; the silvered surfaces are poor emitters of thermal radiation [1]; they also reflect radiation back towards the hot contents, so little energy is lost by radiation [1].
physics12a1-wien-33

Betelgeuse has a surface temperature of about 3500 K and Rigel about 12 000 K. Calculate the peak wavelength of each (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K) and use your results to explain why Betelgeuse appears red while Rigel appears blue-white. (4 marks)

Betelgeuse: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 3500 = 8.28 × 10⁻⁷ m [1]; Rigel: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 12 000 = 2.42 × 10⁻⁷ m [1]; Betelgeuse's peak is in the infrared with its visible output strongest at the red end, so it appears red [1]; Rigel's peak is in the ultraviolet with strong output at the blue end of the visible, so it appears blue-white [1].
physics12a1-wien-34

The spectrum of a blackbody has its peak at 1.2 µm. (a) Calculate its temperature (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K). (b) The temperature is then raised by 1000 K. Calculate the new peak wavelength. (3 marks)
physics12a1-wien-35
Calculate the peak wavelength of the thermal radiation emitted by boiling water at 100 °C (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K) and state the region of the electromagnetic spectrum in which it lies. (3 marks)
T = 100 + 273 = 373 K [1]; λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 373 = 7.77 × 10⁻⁶ m [1]; this is in the infrared region [1].
physics12a1-wien-36
Define a blackbody and explain why a small hole in the wall of a closed, hollow cavity behaves very nearly like one. (3 marks)

A blackbody is an ideal object that absorbs all radiation incident on it and emits the maximum possible thermal radiation at its temperature [1]; radiation entering the small hole is reflected many times inside the cavity and is almost completely absorbed, so almost none escapes [1]; the radiation leaving the hole has a spectrum that depends only on the cavity temperature [1].
physics12a1-wien-37

A thermal imaging camera views a cup of tea at 80 °C in a room at 20 °C. Calculate the peak wavelength emitted by the tea (constant 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K) and explain why the cup appears brighter in the image than the room. (4 marks)

T = 80 + 273 = 353 K [1]; λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 353 = 8.21 × 10⁻⁶ m, in the infrared [1]; the hotter tea emits more infrared radiation per second than its surroundings [1]; the camera detects this greater intensity so the cup appears brighter [1].
vce-physics12-tw-c1
A star's emission peaks at 500 nm. Using λ(max)T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K, its surface temperature is about:
T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ ÷ 500 × 10⁻⁹ = 5800 K. By contrast, Earth (about 288 K) peaks near 10 µm, in the infrared.
vce-physics12-climate-and-the-enhanced-g: physics12a1-gh-1
Which of the following is a greenhouse gas?
methane, CH₄
argon, Ar
nitrogen, N₂
oxygen, O₂
Methane absorbs infrared radiation. The main components of air (N₂, O₂, Ar) do not significantly absorb infrared.
physics12a1-gh-2
Which statement best describes the natural greenhouse effect?
Greenhouse gases absorb visible light from the Sun and reflect it back to space
Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth and re-emit it in all directions, some returning to the surface
Greenhouse gases block all radiation from escaping the atmosphere
Greenhouse gases trap warm air near the ground and stop convection
The Earth's surface re-emits absorbed sunlight as infrared. Greenhouse gases absorb this and re-emit in all directions, so part is returned to the surface, warming it.
physics12a1-gh-3
The enhanced greenhouse effect is the
cooling caused by volcanic eruptions
variation in solar output over 11-year cycles
natural warming caused by water vapour in the atmosphere
additional warming caused by increased concentrations of greenhouse gases from human activity
The enhanced greenhouse effect refers to extra warming from increased greenhouse gas concentrations, e.g. from burning fossil fuels and land clearing.
physics12a1-gh-4
As Arctic sea ice melts, the Earth's albedo in that region decreases. The most likely consequence is
more sunlight absorbed, which warms the region further (a positive feedback)
no change in the energy absorbed
greater cloud formation that cancels the effect entirely
more sunlight reflected, which cools the region
Ice is highly reflective; open ocean is dark and absorbs more radiation. This causes further warming and melting: a positive feedback.
physics12a1-gh-5
If the average rate at which the Earth absorbs solar energy exceeds the average rate at which it radiates energy to space, the Earth's average temperature will
fall to absolute zero
decrease until the rates are equal
increase until the rates are equal again
remain unchanged
A net energy gain raises the temperature. The Earth then radiates more strongly until a new equilibrium is reached.
physics12a1-gh-6
Distinguish between the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect, and state why the natural effect is important to life on Earth. (3 marks)

Natural greenhouse effect: warming from greenhouse gases that occur naturally in the atmosphere (e.g. H₂O, CO₂, CH₄); enhanced: additional warming due to increased greenhouse gas concentrations from human activity such as fossil fuel combustion; the natural effect keeps the Earth's average surface temperature at about 288 K (15 °C) rather than about 255 K (−18 °C), allowing liquid water.
physics12a1-gh-7
Explain two ways global warming leads to a rise in sea level. (3 marks)

Thermal expansion: as the oceans warm, the water expands, increasing its volume; melting of land-based ice (glaciers and ice sheets, e.g. Greenland and Antarctica) adds water to the oceans; floating sea ice contributes little because it already displaces its own mass of water (any two, with explanation).
physics12a1-gh-8
The Sun's radiation peaks at about 500 nm, whereas the Earth's emitted radiation peaks at about 10 µm. Explain how this difference helps account for the greenhouse effect. (3 marks)

Sunlight is mostly visible and passes through the atmosphere largely unabsorbed to heat the surface; the Earth, at a much lower temperature, emits at longer wavelengths (infrared, by Wien's law); greenhouse gases absorb infrared strongly, trapping energy and re-emitting some back to the surface.
physics12a1-gh-9
Which gas makes the largest contribution to the natural greenhouse effect?
water vapour, H₂O
carbon dioxide, CO₂
methane, CH₄
ozone, O₃

Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas and contributes the most to the natural effect. CO₂ is the most important of the gases that humans are increasing, but it is not the largest natural contributor.
physics12a1-gh-10
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas but nitrogen is not. The main reason is that
carbon dioxide is denser than nitrogen and sinks to the surface
the vibration frequencies of carbon dioxide molecules match infrared frequencies, so they absorb it, whereas N₂ does not
carbon dioxide absorbs visible light from the Sun but nitrogen does not
carbon dioxide is present in much larger quantities than nitrogen
CO₂ molecules have vibrational modes that absorb infrared radiation, whereas diatomic N₂ essentially does not. Nitrogen is in fact far more abundant than CO₂, so quantity is not the reason.
physics12a1-gh-11
The albedo of a surface is defined as the
fraction of incident radiation that is absorbed by the surface
temperature of the surface divided by the temperature of the Sun
fraction of incident radiation that is reflected by the surface
power emitted by the surface per unit area
Albedo is the ratio of reflected to incident radiation, so a value near 1 means a highly reflective surface. The absorbed fraction is 1 minus the albedo, which is a common mix-up.
physics12a1-gh-12
Wien's law gives λ_max = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K ÷ T. The Earth's surface has an average temperature of about 288 K. The wavelength at which it emits most strongly is closest to
1.0 µm
100 µm
10 µm
λ_max = 2.898 × 10⁻³ ÷ 288 ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ m = 10 µm, which is in the infrared. Forgetting to convert metres to micrometres gives the tempting wrong values.
physics12a1-gh-13

The power radiated per unit area by a surface is proportional to T⁴, where T is its absolute temperature. If the absolute temperature of a surface is doubled, the power it radiates per unit area increases by a factor of
Doubling T multiplies T⁴ by 2⁴ = 16. A factor of 2 would apply only if power were directly proportional to T.
physics12a1-gh-14
Which human activity is a major source of atmospheric methane?
cement production
raising livestock such as cattle and sheep
burning of hydrogen fuel
use of solar panels
Ruminant livestock, rice paddies, landfill and fossil fuel extraction release methane. Cement production mainly releases CO₂, not methane.
physics12a1-gh-15
Scientists can estimate carbon dioxide concentrations from hundreds of thousands of years ago by analysing
the colour of the sea ice at the poles
the thickness of the current Antarctic ice shelves only
air bubbles trapped in layers of ice cores
the number of days with snowfall each year

Air trapped in bubbles in deep polar ice is a sample of the ancient atmosphere, and isotope ratios in the ice give past temperatures. Surface features of present-day ice cannot give past gas concentrations.
physics12a1-gh-16
Which of the following is an example of a positive feedback in the climate system?
Warmer air holds more water vapour, which forms clouds that cool the surface to exactly cancel the warming
Increased plant growth removes CO₂ and cools the Earth
Increased evaporation causes more rainfall that cools the oceans
Warmer oceans dissolve less CO₂, so more CO₂ stays in the atmosphere and causes further warming
Gases are less soluble in warmer water, so warming releases CO₂ that causes more warming, which amplifies the original change. The other options describe processes that reduce or oppose warming.
physics12a1-gh-17
As the Earth warms, more water evaporates into the atmosphere. Because water vapour is a greenhouse gas, this process
amplifies the warming, acting as a positive feedback
reduces the warming, acting as a negative feedback
has no effect on temperature because water vapour is a natural gas
only affects the albedo of the polar regions
More water vapour absorbs more infrared radiation, increasing warming and so increasing evaporation further. Being natural does not stop water vapour from absorbing infrared.
physics12a1-gh-18
Increased atmospheric CO₂ also affects the oceans. When CO₂ dissolves in seawater, the ocean becomes
more alkaline, because carbon dioxide is a base
more acidic, because carbonic acid forms
warmer by the energy released as the gas dissolves
less dense, so the sea level falls
Dissolved CO₂ reacts with water to form carbonic acid, lowering the pH of seawater (ocean acidification). Carbon dioxide is acidic, not basic.
physics12a1-gh-19

The solar constant (intensity of sunlight at the top of the atmosphere, facing the Sun) is about 1361 W m⁻². Sunlight is intercepted by the Earth's cross-sectional disc, of area πR², but spread over the whole sphere, of area 4πR². The average incident intensity over the whole Earth is closest to
680 W m⁻²
340 W m⁻²
The sphere's area is four times the disc's area, so the average is 1361 ÷ 4 ≈ 340 W m⁻². Dividing by 2 would wrongly assume the sphere is only twice the disc area.
physics12a1-gh-20
The Earth's average incident solar intensity is about 340 W m⁻² and its average albedo is 0.30. The average intensity absorbed by the Earth–atmosphere system is closest to
340 W m⁻²
102 W m⁻²
30 W m⁻²
238 W m⁻²
Absorbed = (1 − 0.30) × 340 = 238 W m⁻². The value 102 W m⁻² is the reflected portion (0.30 × 340), which is a common mistake.
physics12a1-gh-21

The volume of water in a layer of ocean increases by a fraction of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ for each 1 K rise in temperature. A 1000 m deep layer covering a fixed area warms uniformly by 0.50 K. The increase in the height of the sea surface is closest to
Fractional change = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.50 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴, so the rise is 1000 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.10 m. Using the full 1 K instead of 0.50 K would give 0.20 m.
physics12a1-gh-22

Satellite measurements show the Earth absorbs about 0.80 W m⁻² more than it radiates to space, averaged over its surface of area 5.1 × 10¹⁴ m². The net rate at which energy is being gained is closest to
Power = 0.80 × 5.1 × 10¹⁴ = 4.1 × 10¹⁴ W. The other values come from errors in the powers of ten or in the multiplication.
physics12a1-gh-23
Thawing of Arctic permafrost releases trapped methane and carbon dioxide. Which statement about this process is correct?
It is a negative feedback because it removes greenhouse gases from the air
It is not a feedback because humans did not release the gases directly
It is a positive feedback because warming releases greenhouse gases that cause further warming
It has no effect because methane does not absorb infrared radiation

Warming thaws permafrost, which releases greenhouse gases and causes more warming, so the effect is amplified. A feedback is any process driven by the change that in turn affects that change, whether or not humans started it.
physics12a1-gh-24
Large volcanic eruptions can lower global average temperatures for a year or two. This is mainly because
