volcanoes release large amounts of water vapour that absorbs infrared
the heat of the lava absorbs energy from the atmosphere
ash and sulfate aerosols in the upper atmosphere absorb all infrared from the Earth
aerosols reflect incoming sunlight back to space, increasing the albedo
Sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere reflect sunlight, so less energy reaches the surface. Eruptions do release some CO₂ but not enough to offset this short-term cooling.
physics12a1-gh-25
The pre-industrial atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide was about 280 ppm. This means that in every
1 000 000 molecules of air, about 280 are CO₂
1000 molecules of air, about 280 are CO₂
100 molecules of air, about 280 are CO₂
1 000 000 000 molecules of air, about 280 are CO₂
ppm means parts per million, so 280 ppm is 280 molecules of CO₂ per million molecules of air. Confusing ppm with a percentage would greatly overestimate the amount.
physics12a1-gh-26
Which of the following surfaces has the highest albedo?
open ocean water
fresh snow
dark forest
bare dark soil
Fresh snow reflects up to about 80–90% of incident sunlight, whereas ocean, forest and dark soil reflect only a small fraction. This is why loss of snow and ice is significant for warming.
physics12a1-gh-27
Which statement correctly distinguishes weather from climate?
Weather refers to the average temperature of the whole Earth, and climate to a single region
Climate describes conditions only in the polar regions
Climate is the average of weather conditions over a long period, typically decades, whereas weather is the state of the atmosphere over a short period
Weather and climate are the same thing measured in different units
Climate is the long-term statistical pattern of weather, usually averaged over about 30 years. A single cold day is weather and says little about the climate trend.
physics12a1-gh-28
Describe how burning fossil fuels contributes to the enhanced greenhouse effect. (2 marks)

Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas) into the atmosphere, increasing its concentration [1]; the extra greenhouse gas absorbs and re-emits more of the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth, returning more energy to the surface and raising the average temperature [1].
physics12a1-gh-29

A planet's surface has an average temperature of 330 K. Use Wien's law, λ_max = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K ÷ T, to calculate the wavelength at which the surface emits most strongly, and state the region of the electromagnetic spectrum. (2 marks)
λ_max = 2.898 × 10⁻³ ÷ 330 = 8.8 × 10⁻⁶ m (8.8 µm) [1]; this is in the infrared region [1].
physics12a1-gh-30
Explain how ice cores provide evidence of past atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations and past temperatures. (3 marks)

Snow compacts into ice and traps small bubbles of air from the time it fell [1]; analysing the gas in the bubbles at different depths gives past CO₂ concentrations, with deeper ice being older [1]; the ratios of isotopes (e.g. oxygen or hydrogen) in the ice depend on the temperature at the time, giving past temperatures [1].
physics12a1-gh-31
Explain what is meant by a positive feedback in the climate system, using the thawing of permafrost as an example. (3 marks)

A positive feedback is a process in which an initial change causes a further change in the same direction, amplifying the original effect [1]; warming thaws permafrost, releasing trapped methane and CO₂ [1]; these greenhouse gases enhance warming, causing more thawing [1].
physics12a1-gh-32
Using the idea of energy balance, explain why an increase in the concentration of atmospheric CO₂ leads to a rise in the Earth's average surface temperature. (4 marks)

At equilibrium, the rate at which the Earth absorbs solar energy equals the rate at which it radiates energy to space [1]; extra CO₂ absorbs more of the infrared emitted by the surface and re-emits some back downward, so less energy escapes to space [1]; absorbed energy now exceeds energy radiated, so the Earth gains energy and its temperature rises [1]; as it warms, it emits more radiation until emitted and absorbed rates are equal again at a higher temperature [1].
physics12a1-gh-33

A 800 m deep layer of ocean covering a fixed area warms uniformly by 0.80 K. The volume of water increases by a fraction of 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ for each 1 K rise in temperature. Calculate the rise in sea level due to thermal expansion of this layer. (3 marks)

Fractional increase in volume = 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.80 = 1.68 × 10⁻⁴ [1]; for a fixed area, the fractional change in depth equals the fractional change in volume [1]; rise = 800 × 1.68 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.13 m [1].
physics12a1-gh-34
The Earth absorbs 0.60 W m⁻² more energy than it radiates, averaged over its surface of area 5.1 × 10¹⁴ m². Calculate the extra energy gained by the Earth in one year (3.15 × 10⁷ s). (3 marks)
physics12a1-gh-35
Explain how the increase in atmospheric CO₂ affects the chemistry of the oceans, and why this is a concern. (2 marks)

CO₂ dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid, lowering the pH of the oceans (ocean acidification) [1]; this makes it harder for organisms such as corals and shellfish to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons, threatening marine ecosystems [1].
physics12a1-gh-36
Contrast the way a large volcanic eruption and increased CO₂ emissions each affect the Earth's average temperature. (3 marks)

A large eruption injects sulfate aerosols into the upper atmosphere that reflect incoming sunlight, increasing albedo and cooling the Earth [1]; this effect is short lived (a year or two) as the aerosols settle out [1]; increased CO₂ absorbs infrared emitted by the Earth, trapping more energy and causing long-lasting warming [1].
physics12a1-gh-37
A student argues that an unusually cold week in winter proves that global warming is not occurring. Use the terms weather and climate to evaluate this claim. (3 marks)

A cold week is a short-term weather event, the state of the atmosphere over a short time [1]; climate is the average of weather over long periods (decades), so global warming is assessed from long-term trends in average temperature [1]; a single cold week is consistent with warming because short-term variation occurs about a rising average, so the claim is not valid [1].
vce-physics12-cg-c1
Greenhouse gases warm the Earth mainly because they:
Absorb most of the incoming visible sunlight before it can reach the Earth's surface
Make a hole in the ozone layer, which lets extra infrared radiation reach the surface
Reflect all incoming ultraviolet radiation back down, heating the lower atmosphere
Absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and re-emit some of it back towards the surface
Sunlight (mostly visible) passes through; the warmed surface emits infrared, which CO₂, methane and water vapour absorb. More of these gases enhances the effect.
vce-physics12-wave-model-of-light: physics12a1-wave-1
Light has a frequency of 6.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz in a vacuum. Its wavelength is (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
physics12a1-wave-2
Diffraction of light as it passes through a single slit is most noticeable when
the slit is made of metal
the slit width is much larger than the wavelength
the slit width is comparable to the wavelength
the light is white
Diffraction is significant when the opening is of the same order of magnitude as the wavelength.
physics12a1-wave-3
The fact that light can be polarised provides evidence that light is
a transverse wave
a particle only
a sound wave
a longitudinal wave
Only transverse waves, which oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel, can be polarised.
physics12a1-wave-4
Light passes from air into glass. Which of the following describes the changes in speed, wavelength and frequency?
speed unchanged, wavelength decreases, frequency increases
speed increases, wavelength increases, frequency unchanged
speed decreases, wavelength decreases, frequency unchanged
speed decreases, wavelength unchanged, frequency decreases
Frequency is set by the source and does not change. Light slows in glass, so v = fλ shows the wavelength decreases.
physics12a1-wave-5
Two coherent light waves meet at point P, having travelled paths that differ by 1.5 wavelengths. The interference at P is
constructive, giving a bright region
destructive, giving a dark region
neither constructive nor destructive
constructive only if the light is polarised
A path difference of (n + ½)λ gives waves exactly out of phase, so destructive interference. A whole number of wavelengths would give constructive interference.
physics12a1-wave-6

Light of wavelength 650 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.50. Calculate (a) the frequency of the light, (b) the speed of the light in the glass, and (c) the wavelength of the light in the glass. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (3 marks)
physics12a1-wave-7

Light passes through two polarising filters in turn. Describe what happens to the intensity of the transmitted light as the second filter is rotated through 90° from the position where its axis is parallel to the first, and explain why sound waves cannot be polarised. (3 marks)

Intensity is a maximum when axes are parallel and decreases to (almost) zero when the filters are at 90° (crossed); this occurs because only the component of the light's oscillation along the transmission axis passes through; sound is a longitudinal wave, whose oscillations are along the direction of travel, so there is no transverse direction to filter.
physics12a1-wave-8
Explain why diffraction of light is not noticed when light passes through an ordinary doorway, but diffraction of sound is. Give approximate magnitudes in your answer. (3 marks)

Diffraction is significant when the opening is comparable to the wavelength; visible light has a wavelength of about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m, far smaller than a doorway (about 1 m), so there is negligible spreading; audible sound has wavelengths of about 0.1 m to several metres, comparable to the doorway, so it diffracts noticeably.
physics12a1-wave-9
Which statement correctly describes an electromagnetic wave such as light?
It consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
It consists of an oscillating electric field only, parallel to the direction of travel
It consists of compressions and rarefactions of a medium
It can only travel through a material medium
Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave with electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. Unlike sound, it needs no medium.
physics12a1-wave-10
Which of the following regions of the electromagnetic spectrum has the longest wavelength?
X-rays
Microwaves
Visible light
Ultraviolet
Of these, microwaves have the longest wavelength (about 10⁻³ m to 10⁻¹ m). X-rays and ultraviolet are shorter than visible light.
physics12a1-wave-11
Red light has a wavelength of 700 nm in a vacuum. Its frequency is (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 7.00 × 10⁻⁷ = 4.29 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The 10¹⁷ option comes from forgetting to convert nanometres correctly.
physics12a1-wave-12
The refractive index of diamond is 2.42. The speed of light in diamond is closest to (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
v = c/n = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 2.42 = 1.24 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Multiplying by n would give a speed greater than c, which is impossible.
physics12a1-wave-13
Young's double-slit experiment is considered evidence for the wave model of light because it showed
a pattern of alternating bright and dark fringes caused by interference
two bright bands directly behind the two slits
that light travels in straight lines
that light slows down in glass
Alternating bright and dark fringes can only be explained by interference of waves. A particle model predicts just two bright bands behind the slits.
physics12a1-wave-14
In a double-slit experiment the two slits are moved closer together, with everything else unchanged. The fringe spacing on the screen will
decrease
increase
stay the same
increase only for the central fringe
Fringe spacing Δx = λL/d, so decreasing the slit separation d increases Δx. Larger spacing is the opposite of the decrease tempting from 'closer together'.
physics12a1-wave-15
In a double-slit experiment, red light is replaced with blue light and nothing else is changed. The fringe spacing will
increase, because blue light has a higher frequency
stay the same, because the slits are unchanged
decrease, because blue light has a shorter wavelength
disappear, because blue light cannot be diffracted
Δx = λL/d and blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, so the fringes are closer together. Higher frequency does not increase spacing.
physics12a1-wave-16
Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.20 mm apart. The screen is 1.5 m away. The spacing between adjacent bright fringes is
Δx = λL/d = (6.00 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.5) / (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 4.5 × 10⁻³ m. Forgetting to convert 0.20 mm to metres gives 4.5 × 10⁻⁶ m.
physics12a1-wave-17
In a double-slit experiment, a dark fringe forms at a point on the screen because
a crest from one slit arrives together with a trough from the other slit
light cannot reach that point from either slit
the light from the two slits is absorbed by the screen
a crest from one slit arrives together with a crest from the other slit
Dark fringes are regions of destructive interference, where waves arrive out of phase. Light does reach that point from both slits; it cancels there.
physics12a1-wave-18
Which statement best describes the single-slit diffraction pattern of monochromatic light?
Equally bright fringes of equal width
A central bright maximum that is wider and brighter than the other maxima
A central dark band flanked by bright bands
Two bright bands directly in line with the slit edges
The central maximum is the brightest and about twice as wide as the others. Equal fringes are characteristic of a double slit, not a single slit.
physics12a1-wave-19
A single slit is made narrower while the light source stays the same. The central bright region on the screen
becomes narrower
does not change
becomes wider
becomes dimmer but keeps the same width
Diffraction is more pronounced as the slit width approaches the wavelength, so the light spreads more and the central maximum widens.
physics12a1-wave-20
Polarised light is light in which
the wavelength has been reduced
the waves have all been made longitudinal
the frequency has been fixed at a single value
the oscillations of the electric field lie in a single plane
Polarisation restricts the transverse oscillations to one plane. It does not change wavelength or frequency.
physics12a1-wave-21
Unpolarised light passes through a single ideal polarising filter. Compared with the incident light, the transmitted intensity is about
one half
zero
the same
one quarter
Half of the randomly oriented oscillations (the components along the transmission axis) pass through. All of it would pass only if it was already polarised along the axis.
physics12a1-wave-22
Two polarising filters are crossed at 90°. A third filter is placed between them with its axis at 45° to each. What happens to the light reaching the observer?
No light is transmitted, because the first two filters are crossed
Some light is transmitted
All of the light is transmitted
The light becomes unpolarised again
The middle filter rotates the plane of polarisation by 45°, so the light has a component along the axis of the last filter. Crossed filters alone block light, but the third filter changes this.
physics12a1-wave-23
Polarising sunglasses reduce glare from a horizontal water surface. This works because reflected light is
mostly of a single colour, which the lenses absorb
longitudinally polarised, which the lenses block
partially polarised mostly in the horizontal plane, and the lenses have a vertical transmission axis
unpolarised, and the lenses halve its intensity
Reflection from a horizontal surface partially polarises light in the horizontal plane. Vertical-axis lenses block most of it, while light waves cannot be longitudinal.
physics12a1-wave-24
Two light sources are said to be coherent if they
have the same intensity
are the same colour as seen by the eye
are placed close together
emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference
Coherence requires the same frequency and a fixed phase relationship. Matching colour or brightness does not guarantee a constant phase difference.
physics12a1-wave-25
Two separate light globes placed next to each other do not produce a visible interference pattern because
their light is not coherent, as the phase difference varies randomly
light from different sources never interferes
the wavelengths of the globes are too long
the light from globes is polarised
The atoms in each globe emit light with randomly changing phase, so there is no stable phase difference. Interference still occurs, but it averages out too rapidly to see.
physics12a1-wave-26
Light of wavelength 532 nm in air enters water of refractive index 1.33. The wavelength in water is closest to
708 nm
400 nm
532 nm
λ in water = λ in air / n = 532 / 1.33 = 400 nm. The frequency is unchanged, so the wavelength shrinks; 532 nm would imply no change.
physics12a1-wave-27
Visible light of different colours passes through the same narrow slit. Which colour is diffracted (spread) the most?
Violet
Blue
Red
Green
Red has the longest wavelength of these, and diffraction is greatest when the wavelength is large compared with the slit width.
physics12a1-wave-28
Define what is meant by coherent light sources, and explain why the two slits in Young's experiment must act as coherent sources. (2 marks)

Coherent sources emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference [1]; both slits are illuminated by the same wavefront from one source, so they keep a fixed phase relationship and produce a stable interference pattern [1].
physics12a1-wave-29
Light of wavelength 550 nm passes through a double slit with a slit separation of 0.25 mm. A screen is placed 2.0 m from the slits. Calculate the spacing between adjacent bright fringes. (3 marks)
physics12a1-wave-30
Explain how a double slit produces a pattern of bright and dark fringes on a screen. (3 marks)

Light diffracts at each slit so that waves spread out and overlap [1]; where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively, giving a bright fringe [1]; where the path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths they arrive out of phase and interfere destructively, giving a dark fringe [1].
physics12a1-wave-31

Coherent light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits. At point P on the screen, the distances from the two slits differ by 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ m. Determine whether P is a bright or dark fringe, showing your working. (2 marks)
Path difference in wavelengths = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ / 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ = 4.0 [1]; a whole number of wavelengths means constructive interference, so P is a bright fringe [1].
physics12a1-wave-32

A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 100 MHz. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves, and explain why radio waves of this frequency diffract around buildings while visible light does not. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (3 marks)

λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.00 × 10⁸ = 3.0 m [1]; diffraction is significant when the obstacle or opening is comparable in size to the wavelength [1]; radio wavelengths (metres) are comparable to buildings, whereas visible light (about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m) is far smaller, so it shows negligible diffraction [1].
physics12a1-wave-33
A double-slit experiment is set up in air and then the whole apparatus is immersed in water without changing anything else. Describe and explain the change in the fringe spacing. (3 marks)

The fringe spacing decreases [1]; the frequency stays the same but the speed of light is lower in water, so the wavelength decreases [1]; since Δx = λL/d, a smaller λ gives a smaller fringe spacing [1].
physics12a1-wave-34

In a double-slit experiment the slit separation is 0.30 mm and the screen is 1.8 m from the slits. The spacing between adjacent bright fringes is measured to be 3.6 mm. Calculate the wavelength of the light. (3 marks)
vce-physics12-wm-c1
A radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. The wavelength of its waves is:
λ = c/f = 3.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁸ = 3.0 m. Remember that mega means 10⁶.
vce-physics12-the-electromagnetic-spectr: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum has the highest frequency?
In order of increasing frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
All electromagnetic waves travelling in a vacuum have the same
All electromagnetic waves travel at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum. Frequency and wavelength differ across the spectrum.
A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 100 MHz. The wavelength of its waves in air is closest to
Which pairing of radiation and application is correct?
X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, so they are used for bone imaging. Remote controls use infrared; fractures are imaged by X-rays rather than radio waves.
Light of wavelength 450 nm is in which region of the electromagnetic spectrum?
The visible region is roughly 400 nm to 700 nm; 450 nm is blue-violet visible light.
(a) List the seven main regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency. (b) State how the frequency and wavelength of an electromagnetic wave are related. (3 marks)
(a) radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma (all in correct order for 2 marks); (b) c = fλ, so frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength (constant speed in a vacuum).
An X-ray has a wavelength of 0.100 nm. (a) Calculate its frequency. (b) Calculate the time taken for light from the Sun to reach Earth, a distance of 1.50 × 10¹¹ m. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (3 marks)
Explain why ultraviolet radiation is more harmful to living tissue than visible light, and describe one way humans are protected from it. (3 marks)

Ultraviolet has a higher frequency (shorter wavelength) so each photon carries more energy; this energy can damage DNA and cells (e.g. sunburn, skin cancer) whereas visible light photons do not; protection: the ozone layer absorbs UV, or sunscreen, clothing and sunglasses absorb or block it.
Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum has the longest wavelengths?
Wavelength increases as frequency decreases, so radio waves, at the low-frequency end of the spectrum, have the longest wavelengths. Microwaves are longer than infrared but shorter than radio.
Green light has a wavelength of 530 nm in a vacuum. Its frequency is closest to
f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 5.30 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.66 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Multiplying c by λ instead of dividing gives a meaningless result.
Microwave ovens heat food mainly because the microwaves are
reflected by the water molecules in the food
converted to infrared by the oven walls
absorbed by water molecules in the food, increasing their thermal energy
ionising the molecules in the food
Water molecules in the food absorb the microwave energy, which raises their thermal energy. Microwaves are non-ionising, so they do not ionise the food.
A thermal imaging camera forms an image of a person in complete darkness by detecting
visible light reflected from the person
ultraviolet radiation emitted by the person
radio waves emitted by the person
infrared radiation emitted by the person
Objects at body temperature emit infrared radiation, which the camera detects. Reflected visible light is absent in the dark.
A microwave oven operates at a frequency of 2.45 GHz. The wavelength of its microwaves is closest to
λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 2.45 × 10⁹ = 0.122 m. Dividing f by c gives 8.17, which is not a wavelength.
The frequency of an electromagnetic wave travelling in a vacuum is doubled. Its wavelength
Since c = fλ and c is constant in a vacuum, wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency. Doubling f halves λ.
Which of the following is NOT an electromagnetic wave?
Ultrasound is a mechanical sound wave that needs a medium, whereas electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum.
Electromagnetic waves are best described as
transverse waves of oscillating electric and magnetic fields
Electromagnetic waves are transverse, with electric and magnetic fields oscillating perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. They are not particle streams and need no medium.
Light has a frequency of 6.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Its wavelength in a vacuum is
λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 6.00 × 10¹⁴ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m (500 nm). Dividing f by c gives 2.00 × 10⁶, which is not a wavelength.
A radio signal is sent from the ground to a geostationary satellite 3.60 × 10⁷ m away. The time taken for the signal to reach the satellite is
t = d/c = 3.60 × 10⁷ / 3.00 × 10⁸ = 0.120 s. Inverting the ratio gives 8.33, which is wrong.
Gamma rays are used in medicine mainly for
Gamma rays are highly energetic ionising radiation that can kill cells and microbes. Forged banknotes are checked with UV and satellite communication uses radio or microwaves.
Some banknotes carry ink that glows visibly under an ultraviolet lamp. This occurs because the ink
absorbs ultraviolet and re-emits it as visible light
transmits ultraviolet without interacting with it
Fluorescent inks absorb ultraviolet photons and re-emit lower-energy visible light. Re-emitting at a higher energy such as X-rays would be impossible.
Radiation with a wavelength of 10 μm lies in which region of the electromagnetic spectrum?
10 μm = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ m, which is longer than visible light (700 nm) but much shorter than microwaves, so it is infrared.
Mobile phone networks transmit signals using mainly
Mobile phones communicate using microwaves, which carry information over long distances through the atmosphere. Ultraviolet and gamma rays are ionising and unsuitable.
Which list is in order of increasing wavelength?
gamma rays, ultraviolet, infrared, radio waves
radio waves, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma rays
ultraviolet, gamma rays, radio waves, infrared
infrared, ultraviolet, radio waves, gamma rays
Wavelength increases as frequency decreases, so the order is gamma, ultraviolet, infrared, radio. The second list is in order of decreasing wavelength.
Electromagnetic radiation with a frequency of 1.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz belongs to which region?
λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.0 × 10¹⁰ = 0.030 m (3 cm), which is the microwave region. Infrared and visible light have wavelengths of micrometres or less.
State two properties that all electromagnetic waves share in a vacuum, and state one property that differs between different regions of the spectrum. (3 marks)

They all travel at the same speed, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ [1]; they are all transverse waves of oscillating electric and magnetic fields (and can travel through a vacuum) [1]; frequency (or wavelength, or photon energy) differs between regions [1].
Describe how infrared radiation is produced by everyday objects and give one application that uses it. (2 marks)

All objects above absolute zero emit infrared radiation, with warmer objects emitting more, due to the thermal motion of their particles [1]; application, e.g. thermal imaging cameras, remote controls or infrared heaters [1].
Distinguish between ionising and non-ionising electromagnetic radiation, naming one region of each type. (3 marks)

Ionising radiation has photons with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms or molecules [1]; non-ionising radiation does not have enough energy to do so [1]; examples: ionising: ultraviolet (high end), X-rays or gamma rays; non-ionising: radio, microwave, infrared or visible [1].
Explain how an X-ray image of a broken arm is formed. (3 marks)

X-rays are directed through the arm onto a detector or film [1]; bone absorbs more X-rays than soft tissue, so fewer X-rays reach the detector behind the bone [1]; this produces contrast, with the bone appearing as a different brightness from the surrounding tissue, so the fracture is visible [1].
A radar pulse is sent from an airport and its echo returns after 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ s. Calculate the distance to the aircraft. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (3 marks)
Total distance travelled = ct = 3.00 × 10⁸ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.2 × 10⁵ m [1]; this is a round trip, so divide by 2 [1]; distance = 6.0 × 10⁴ m (60 km) [1].
Compare gamma rays and radio waves in terms of frequency, wavelength and photon energy. (3 marks)
Gamma rays have a much higher frequency than radio waves [1]; gamma rays have a much shorter wavelength than radio waves [1]; gamma-ray photons carry much more energy than radio-wave photons [1].
Give two uses of ultraviolet radiation and identify the property of ultraviolet that makes each use possible. (2 marks)

Sterilising water or equipment, because ultraviolet photons have enough energy to damage the DNA of microbes [1]; detecting forged banknotes (or fluorescence), because certain materials absorb ultraviolet and re-emit visible light [1].
The visible spectrum extends from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Calculate the frequency at each end and state which end has the higher frequency. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (4 marks)
f = c/λ [1]; violet: 3.00 × 10⁸ / 4.00 × 10⁻⁷ = 7.50 × 10¹⁴ Hz [1]; red: 3.00 × 10⁸ / 7.00 × 10⁻⁷ = 4.29 × 10¹⁴ Hz [1]; violet has the higher frequency (shorter wavelength) [1].
A student claims that radio waves travel faster than visible light because they are used to send signals over long distances. Evaluate this claim. (2 marks)

The claim is incorrect: all electromagnetic waves, including radio and visible light, travel at the same speed c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum [1]; radio waves are used for communication because of their long wavelengths and how they interact with the atmosphere, not because they are faster [1].
A 5G signal uses a frequency of 28.0 GHz, while an older mobile signal uses 700 MHz. Calculate the wavelength of each. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (3 marks)
Which radiation has a longer wavelength than visible light but a shorter wavelength than microwaves?
In order of increasing wavelength: gamma, X-rays, UV, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio.
vce-physics12-refraction-and-snells-law: physics12a1-ref-1
A ray of light in air strikes a glass surface (n = 1.50) at 40° to the normal. The angle of refraction is closest to (n of air = 1.00)
sin θ₂ = (1.00 × sin 40°)/1.50 = 0.6428/1.50 = 0.4285, so θ₂ = 25.4°. 74.6° results from multiplying instead of dividing by n.
physics12a1-ref-2
The speed of light in a transparent liquid is 2.25 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The refractive index of the liquid is (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
physics12a1-ref-3
A ray of light travels from water into air at an oblique angle. The ray
is always totally internally reflected
bends towards the normal
bends away from the normal
continues undeviated
Light speeds up as it enters the lower-index medium (air), so it bends away from the normal.
physics12a1-ref-4
Total internal reflection can occur only when light
travels from a medium of lower refractive index to one of higher refractive index at any angle
travels from a medium of higher refractive index to one of lower refractive index at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
strikes a surface along the normal
travels from air into glass above the critical angle
TIR requires travel from higher n to lower n with an angle of incidence exceeding the critical angle.
physics12a1-ref-5
The critical angle for light travelling from glass (n = 1.50) to air is closest to
physics12a1-ref-6

A ray of light in air strikes the surface of water (n = 1.33) with an angle of incidence of 30.0°. (a) Calculate the angle of refraction. (b) Calculate the speed of light in the water. (c) State whether the ray bends towards or away from the normal. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (4 marks)
(a) sin θ₂ = sin 30.0° / 1.33 = 0.3759, θ₂ = 22.1°; (b) v = c/n = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.33 = 2.26 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; (c) towards the normal, as light slows in the higher-index medium.
physics12a1-ref-7
Diamond has a refractive index of 2.42. (a) Calculate the critical angle for a diamond–air boundary. (b) Explain why a cut diamond sparkles. (3 marks)

(a) sin θc = 1/2.42 = 0.413, so θc = 24.4°; (b) the critical angle is small so light entering the diamond strikes internal surfaces at angles larger than θc and is totally internally reflected many times before exiting through certain faces, producing intense sparkle.
physics12a1-ref-8
A swimming pool appears shallower than its true depth when viewed from above. Explain this using refraction. (3 marks)

Rays from a point on the bottom bend away from the normal as they pass from water into air (lower n); the eye traces the rays back in straight lines to an apparent source position; this apparent position is higher than the real position, so the pool looks shallower.
physics12a1-ref-9
A ray of light in air strikes the surface of water (n = 1.33) at an angle of incidence of 45°. The angle of refraction is closest to
sin θ₂ = sin 45° / 1.33 = 0.7071/1.33 = 0.5316, so θ₂ = 32.1°. 70.1° results from multiplying by 1.33 instead of dividing.
physics12a1-ref-10
Light passes from air into glass. Which quantity does NOT change?
Speed
Wavelength
Frequency
Direction of travel at an oblique angle of incidence
Frequency is set by the source and stays constant across a boundary. Speed and wavelength both decrease in glass, which is what causes the ray to change direction.
physics12a1-ref-11
Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.50. Its wavelength in the glass is
900 nm
600 nm
500 nm
400 nm
Frequency is unchanged and v = c/n, so λ = λ₀/n = 600/1.50 = 400 nm. 900 nm results from multiplying by n instead of dividing.
physics12a1-ref-12
Snell's law for light crossing a boundary from medium 1 to medium 2 is written as
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
n₁ sin θ₂ = n₂ sin θ₁
n₁ cos θ₁ = n₂ cos θ₂
θ₁/θ₂ = n₂/n₁
Snell's law relates the sines of the angles to the refractive indices as n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. The angles themselves are not in simple proportion, so the last option is wrong.
physics12a1-ref-13
A ray travels from water (n = 1.33) into glass (n = 1.50) with an angle of incidence of 30.0°. The angle of refraction is closest to
sin θ₂ = 1.33 × sin 30.0° / 1.50 = 0.4433, so θ₂ = 26.3°. 34.3° comes from inverting the ratio of refractive indices.
physics12a1-ref-14
The critical angle for light travelling from water (n = 1.33) to air is closest to
physics12a1-ref-15
Optical fibres can carry light over long distances with little loss because
the core has a lower refractive index than the cladding
the cladding is coated with a reflective metal
light strikes the core–cladding boundary at angles smaller than the critical angle
the core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, so light is totally internally reflected
Light in the higher-index core meets the core–cladding boundary above the critical angle and is totally internally reflected. A lower-index core could never produce total internal reflection.
physics12a1-ref-16
When light inside a medium strikes a boundary at exactly the critical angle, the refracted ray travels
along the boundary, at 90° to the normal
along the normal, at 0° to the normal
at the same angle as the incident ray
back into the original medium
The critical angle is the angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction is 90°, so the ray skims along the boundary. Beyond it there is no refracted ray.
physics12a1-ref-17
A ray in air strikes a transparent material at 60° to the normal and refracts at 35° to the normal. The refractive index of the material is closest to
n = sin 60° / sin 35° = 0.8660/0.5736 = 1.51. Dividing the angles directly (60/35 = 1.71) is not valid because Snell's law uses sines.
physics12a1-ref-18
When light travels from air into glass, which statement is correct?
Speed increases and wavelength decreases
Speed decreases and frequency decreases
Speed and wavelength both decrease
Speed and wavelength both increase
Light slows in glass and, because frequency is fixed, v = fλ means the wavelength shortens too. Frequency does not decrease.
physics12a1-ref-19
A ray bends towards the normal as it passes from medium X into medium Y. Which statement is correct?
Light travels faster in Y than in X
Y has a lower refractive index than X
The frequency of the light is lower in Y than in X
Light travels slower in Y than in X
Bending towards the normal means Y has the higher refractive index, so light is slower in Y. Frequency stays the same across the boundary.
physics12a1-ref-20
A ray of light in air strikes a glass surface along the normal. The ray
passes into the glass without changing direction but slows down
passes into the glass without changing direction or speed
bends towards the normal and slows down
is totally internally reflected
At 0° incidence sin θ₂ = 0, so the direction is unchanged, but the speed still falls to c/n. Total internal reflection only occurs from higher to lower refractive index.
physics12a1-ref-21
The critical angle for light travelling from glass (n = 1.50) to water (n = 1.33) is closest to
sin θc = 1.33/1.50 = 0.887, so θc = 62.5°. 41.8° is the glass–air value, which does not apply to a glass–water boundary.
physics12a1-ref-22
A ray inside glass (n = 1.50) strikes a glass–air boundary at 30.0° to the normal. The angle of refraction in air is closest to
sin θ₂ = 1.50 × sin 30.0° / 1.00 = 0.750, so θ₂ = 48.6°. 19.5° comes from dividing by 1.50 rather than multiplying.
physics12a1-ref-23
A ray of light passes through a parallel-sided glass block and emerges into air on the opposite face. The emergent ray is
parallel to the incident ray but displaced sideways
parallel to the incident ray and in line with it
bent towards the normal compared with the incident ray
at the critical angle to the normal
The two refractions are equal and opposite, so the final direction matches the original, but the ray is shifted sideways. It is only in line with the original ray when incident along the normal.
physics12a1-ref-24
A ray inside glass (n = 1.50) strikes a glass–air boundary at 45° to the normal. What happens?
It refracts into air at 45° to the normal
It is totally internally reflected, leaving at 45° to the normal
It is totally internally reflected, leaving at 41.8° to the normal
It refracts into air at about 71° to the normal
45° exceeds the critical angle of 41.8°, so no light is refracted. The ray is totally internally reflected and the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
physics12a1-ref-25
No transparent material has a refractive index less than 1 because
light would then bend away from the normal when entering it from air
the frequency would increase in the material
light travels fastest in a vacuum, so v is never greater than c
light cannot be refracted in gases
Since n = c/v and v cannot exceed c in a material, n is at least 1. Frequency does not change at a boundary, so the second option is wrong.
physics12a1-ref-26
A ray of light in air strikes a glass surface (n = 1.52) at an angle of incidence of 35.0°. Calculate the angle of refraction. (2 marks)
physics12a1-ref-27
Yellow light of wavelength 589 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.52. Calculate (a) the speed of the light in the glass and (b) its wavelength in the glass. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (3 marks)
(a) v = c/n = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.52 = 1.97 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ [1]; (b) frequency is unchanged, so λ = λ₀/n = 589/1.52 [1] = 388 nm [1]
physics12a1-ref-28
Explain, in terms of the speed of light, why a ray bends towards the normal when it passes from air into glass at an oblique angle. (2 marks)

Light travels more slowly in glass than in air (higher refractive index) [1]; the part of the wavefront that enters the glass first slows down first, so the wavefront swings and the ray bends towards the normal [1]
physics12a1-ref-29
A glass has a refractive index of 1.60. (a) Calculate the critical angle for a glass–air boundary. (b) State the two conditions needed for total internal reflection at this boundary. (3 marks)
(a) sin θc = 1.00/1.60 = 0.625 [1], θc = 38.7° [1]; (b) light must travel from the higher-index glass towards air, and the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle [1]
physics12a1-ref-30
A ray in water (n = 1.33) strikes a boundary with glass (n = 1.50) at an angle of incidence of 40.0°. Calculate the angle of refraction in the glass. (2 marks)
physics12a1-ref-31
Describe an experiment, using a ray box and a rectangular glass block, to determine the refractive index of the glass. State what is measured and how the result is obtained. (4 marks)

Shine a narrow ray from the ray box into the block at several different angles of incidence, tracing the incident and emergent rays and the block outline on paper [1]; draw the normal and join the entry and exit points to find the refracted ray inside the block [1]; measure the angles of incidence and refraction with a protractor for each trial [1]; plot sin θ₁ against sin θ₂ (or calculate sin θ₁/sin θ₂ for each trial) and the gradient (average) gives the refractive index of the glass [1]
physics12a1-ref-32
Explain how an optical fibre transmits light along its length with very little loss through the sides. (3 marks)

The fibre has a core of higher refractive index surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index [1]; light enters the core and strikes the core–cladding boundary at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle [1]; it is totally internally reflected repeatedly, so none escapes and it travels along the fibre [1]
physics12a1-ref-33
A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the water surface when viewed from the side. Explain why. (2 marks)

Light from the submerged part of the straw bends away from the normal as it passes from water into air [1]; the eye traces these rays back in straight lines, so the submerged part appears at a different (shallower) position from the part in air, making the straw look bent [1]
physics12a1-ref-34

A ray in glass (n = 1.50) strikes a glass–water (n = 1.33) boundary at an angle of incidence of 55.0°. (a) Calculate the angle of refraction in the water. (b) State, with a reason, whether total internal reflection occurs. (3 marks)
(a) sin θ₂ = 1.50 × sin 55.0° / 1.33 = 1.50 × 0.8192/1.33 = 0.9238 [1], θ₂ = 67.5° [1]; (b) no, because the angle of incidence (55.0°) is less than the critical angle sin⁻¹(1.33/1.50) = 62.5° [1]
physics12a1-ref-35

In an experiment, a ray in air strikes a clear plastic block. At an angle of incidence of 20.0° the angle of refraction is 13.0°, and at 40.0° the angle of refraction is 25.0°. Calculate the refractive index from each trial and state the average value. (3 marks)
physics12a1-ref-36

Light of frequency 5.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz travels from air into water (n = 1.33). Determine (a) its wavelength in air, (b) its speed in water, (c) its wavelength in water and (d) its frequency in water. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (4 marks)
physics12a1-ref-37
Explain why a glass prism splits white light into a spectrum of colours. (3 marks)

The refractive index of glass is slightly different for different wavelengths, being larger for violet/blue light than for red light [1]; so on entering the prism each colour is refracted through a different angle (violet bends most, red least) [1]; the separation increases at the second face, producing a spectrum [1]
vce-physics12-rs-c1
Light in air strikes glass (n = 1.50) at an angle of incidence of 40°. Find the angle of refraction.
About 25°
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂: 1.00 × sin 40° = 1.50 × sin θ₂, so sin θ₂ = 0.429 and θ₂ ≈ 25.4°. Light bends towards the normal entering a denser medium.
vce-physics12-total-internal-reflection-: physics12a2-tir-1
Light travels from glass (refractive index 1.50) into air. What is the critical angle for this boundary?
sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1.00/1.50 = 0.667, so θc = 41.8°. 48.2° is the complement (90° − 41.8°), a common slip.
physics12a2-tir-2
Which pair of conditions must BOTH be met for total internal reflection to occur at a boundary?
Light moves from a less dense to a more dense medium, and the angle of incidence is less than the critical angle
Light moves from a more dense to a less dense medium, and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle
Light moves from a more dense to a less dense medium, and the angle of incidence is less than the critical angle
Light moves from a less dense to a more dense medium, and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle

TIR needs the light to be in the higher-refractive-index medium heading towards the lower one, with the angle of incidence exceeding θc. Going into a denser medium the ray always bends towards the normal, so no critical angle exists.
physics12a2-tir-3
White light passes through a glass prism and spreads into a spectrum. Violet light is deviated more than red light because, in glass,
glass has a higher refractive index for violet light than for red light
violet light has a longer wavelength than red light
violet light has a lower frequency than red light
violet light travels faster than red light

Refractive index depends on wavelength: n is larger for violet (shorter wavelength), so violet travels slower in glass and bends more on refraction. Violet has a higher, not lower, frequency and a shorter wavelength.
physics12a2-tir-4
A light ray in air strikes the surface of water (n = 1.33) at an angle of incidence of 40°. What is the angle of refraction?
sin θ₂ = sin 40° / 1.33 = 0.6428 / 1.33 = 0.483, so θ₂ = 28.9°. 30.1° comes from dividing the angle (40°) by 1.33 rather than the sine; 58.8° comes from multiplying by 1.33.
physics12a2-tir-5
An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.48 surrounded by cladding of refractive index 1.46. The cladding has a lower refractive index so that
the light is dispersed into its colours along the fibre
light in the core undergoes total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary
light travels faster in the core than in the cladding
light is refracted out of the core and into the cladding
TIR requires the light to be in the higher-index medium meeting a lower-index one at an angle beyond θc. The lower-index cladding provides this at the boundary, so the signal stays in the core.
physics12a2-tir-6
The refractive index of diamond is 2.42. (a) Calculate the critical angle for a diamond-air boundary. (b) Explain why a cut diamond sparkles. (3 marks)

(a) sin θc = 1/2.42 = 0.413, so θc ≈ 24.4°; (b) the critical angle is small, so most rays inside the diamond strike internal faces at angles greater than θc; they undergo total internal reflection several times before leaving through the top, giving bright sparkle (and dispersion adds colour).
physics12a2-tir-7

Light in glass (n = 1.52) strikes a glass-water (n = 1.33) boundary. (a) Calculate the critical angle. (b) State what happens to a ray with an angle of incidence of 55° and to a ray with an angle of incidence of 65°. (3 marks)

(a) sin θc = 1.33/1.52 = 0.875, so θc ≈ 61°; (b) at 55° (< θc) the ray is partly refracted into the water, bending away from the normal, with a weak partial reflection; at 65° (> θc) there is total internal reflection, so no light enters the water.
physics12a2-tir-8
Explain why a prism disperses white light into a spectrum, and why a rainbow shows red on the outer edge of the primary arc. (3 marks)

White light is a mixture of wavelengths; the refractive index of the glass or water depends on wavelength, being greater for shorter wavelengths; so each colour refracts by a different amount and separates (violet bends most, red least); in a raindrop the red light is deviated least, so it reaches the observer from the higher, outer part of the bow.
vce-physics12-ti-c1
The critical angle for light going from glass (n = 1.50) into air is about:
sin c = n₂/n₁ = 1 ÷ 1.50, so c ≈ 41.8°. Diamond (n = 2.42) has c ≈ 24°, which is why it sparkles.
vce-physics12-nuclear-stability-and-isot: physics12a2-nsi-1
Which statement correctly describes isotopes of an element?
They have the same number of nucleons but different numbers of electrons
They have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
They have the same mass number but different numbers of protons
An element is defined by its proton number Z. Isotopes share Z but differ in neutron number N, and therefore in mass number A.
physics12a2-nsi-2
How many neutrons are in a nucleus of uranium-235 (atomic number 92)?
N = A − Z = 235 − 92 = 143. 92 is the proton number and 235 is the total number of nucleons.
physics12a2-nsi-3
Protons in a nucleus repel each other electrostatically, yet most nuclei are stable. The main reason is
the weak nuclear force, which binds protons to neutrons
the strong nuclear force, which acts attractively between nucleons over very short distances
the gravitational force between nucleons, which exceeds the electrostatic repulsion
the electrons orbiting the nucleus, which screen the repulsion
The strong nuclear force is attractive between nucleons, much stronger than electrostatic repulsion at about 1 fm separation, but has a very short range. Gravity is far too weak at this scale.
physics12a2-nsi-4
For stable nuclei with a high atomic number, the ratio of neutrons to protons is
exactly one
less than one
greater than one
zero
Heavy stable nuclei have more neutrons than protons (N/Z up to about 1.5). Extra neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding electrostatic repulsion, which grows with the number of protons.
physics12a2-nsi-5
On a graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number, which of these nuclei lies closest to the maximum?
Iron-56
Uranium-235
Hydrogen-2
Helium-4
The curve peaks near iron-56 (about 8.8 MeV per nucleon), so it is among the most tightly bound nuclei. Uranium-235 sits lower (about 7.6 MeV) and hydrogen-2 much lower (about 1.1 MeV).
physics12a2-nsi-6
A helium-4 nucleus has a mass defect of 0.0304 u. Taking 1 u to be equivalent to 931.5 MeV, calculate (a) the binding energy of the nucleus and (b) the binding energy per nucleon. (3 marks)
(a) E = 0.0304 × 931.5 ≈ 28.3 MeV; (b) 4 nucleons, so 28.3 / 4 ≈ 7.08 MeV per nucleon (≈ 7.1 MeV).
physics12a2-nsi-7
Carbon has isotopes ¹²C, ¹³C and ¹⁴C (Z = 6). (a) State the number of protons and neutrons in each isotope. (b) ¹⁴C is radioactive while ¹²C and ¹³C are stable. Suggest why. (3 marks)

(a) each has 6 protons; neutrons 6, 7 and 8 respectively; (b) ¹⁴C has too many neutrons for its number of protons (N/Z above the stable band), so the nucleus is unstable; it changes by decay (beta-minus) to reach a more stable ratio.
physics12a2-nsi-8
Explain why large stable nuclei contain more neutrons than protons. (3 marks)

The strong force is attractive but very short range, so each nucleon only attracts its near neighbours; the electrostatic repulsion between protons has a long range and acts between all proton pairs, so it grows faster with size; extra neutrons add strong-force attraction and spread the protons apart without adding repulsion; so heavy nuclei need N > Z to be stable.
vce-physics12-ns-c1
Why do large nuclei need more neutrons than protons to be stable?
Neutrons repel protons, which pushes the protons apart and spreads the charge
Neutrons have a small positive charge, which balances the electron cloud
Extra neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding electrostatic repulsion
Protons are heavier than neutrons, so more neutrons are needed to balance them
The strong force acts only over very short distances, while proton–proton repulsion acts across the whole nucleus.
vce-physics12-alpha-beta-and-gamma-radia: Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?

Alpha particles (helium nuclei) are heavy and highly ionising, so they lose their energy within a few centimetres of air or in paper. Beta needs millimetres of aluminium and gamma needs thick lead or concrete.
Radium-226 (Z = 88) undergoes alpha decay. The daughter nucleus is
An alpha particle is ⁴₂He, so A falls by 4 (226 → 222) and Z falls by 2 (88 → 86). Element 86 is radon.
Cobalt-60 (Z = 27) decays by beta-minus emission. The daughter nucleus has
In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. A stays at 60 and Z rises by 1 to 28 (nickel-60).
A nucleus emits a gamma ray. As a result, the nucleus
gains one proton and loses one neutron
changes neither its mass number nor its atomic number
changes its atomic number but not its mass number
loses two protons and two neutrons
Gamma emission releases excess energy from an excited nucleus, usually after alpha or beta decay. The number and type of nucleons stay the same, so A and Z are unchanged.

The count rate from an unknown source is measured through different absorbers. Paper has almost no effect, 3 mm of aluminium reduces the count to near background, and adding lead causes no further change. The source emits
Paper not reducing the count rules out alpha. Aluminium removing nearly everything rules out significant gamma, which would still penetrate it. This matches beta radiation alone.

Write nuclear equations for (a) the alpha decay of americium-241 (Z = 95) to neptunium (Z = 93) and (b) the beta-minus decay of carbon-14 (Z = 6) to nitrogen (Z = 7). Show the particle emitted in each. (3 marks)
(a) ²⁴¹₉₅Am → ²³⁷₉₃Np + ⁴₂He; (b) ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e + antineutrino (ν̄); mass numbers and atomic numbers balance on both sides in each equation.
Compare alpha, beta and gamma radiation in terms of their ionising ability and their penetrating power. (3 marks)

Alpha: greatest ionising ability (large mass and +2 charge), least penetrating (stopped by paper or a few cm of air); beta: moderate ionising ability, moderate penetration (stopped by a few mm of aluminium); gamma: weakest ionising ability (no charge), most penetrating (needs thick lead or concrete); ionising ability and penetrating power are inversely related.
Smoke detectors commonly contain a small americium-241 source that emits alpha particles. Explain why an alpha emitter is suitable for this use and why it is safe in normal use. (3 marks)

Alpha particles strongly ionise the air in the chamber, producing a steady current between the plates; smoke particles absorb or attach to the ions and reduce the current, triggering the alarm; alpha radiation is stopped by the detector casing and a few cm of air, so little escapes; the source is only dangerous if ingested or inhaled.
An alpha particle is identical to
An alpha particle consists of two protons and two neutrons, which is a helium-4 nucleus. A fast-moving electron is a beta-minus particle, not an alpha particle.
a high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus
an electromagnetic wave from the nucleus
a proton emitted from the nucleus
A β⁻ particle is an electron created when a neutron changes into a proton. It is not an electromagnetic wave, which describes gamma radiation.
Gamma rays are very high-frequency photons with no mass and no charge. They are not particles like alpha or beta, which is why they are the most penetrating.
Uranium-238 (Z = 92) decays by alpha emission. The daughter nucleus is
Emitting ⁴₂He reduces A from 238 to 234 and Z from 92 to 90, giving thorium-234. Keeping A at 238 would ignore the mass carried away by the alpha particle.
Strontium-90 (Z = 38) decays by beta-minus emission. The daughter nucleus is
In β⁻ decay A is unchanged and Z increases by 1, so the daughter has A = 90 and Z = 39 (yttrium). Rubidium would result from a decrease in Z, which does not happen in β⁻ decay.
Compared with an alpha particle, a beta-minus particle has
the same charge but a smaller mass
the opposite sign of charge and a much smaller mass
the same sign of charge and a larger mass
no charge and a much smaller mass
A beta-minus particle is a negative electron with charge −e, whereas an alpha particle has charge +2e. The electron's mass is thousands of times smaller than that of an alpha particle.
A beam of alpha, beta and gamma radiation passes through a strong magnetic field. Which radiation continues in a straight line?
Gamma rays carry no charge, so a magnetic field exerts no force on them. Alpha and beta are charged and are deflected in opposite directions.
Fluorine-18 (Z = 9) decays by beta-plus emission. The daughter nucleus is
In β⁺ decay a proton becomes a neutron, so A stays at 18 and Z falls by 1 to 8 (oxygen-18). Neon-18 would require Z to increase, as in β⁻ decay.
An alpha-emitting source is most hazardous to a person when it is
covered by a layer of clothing

Inside the body alpha particles deposit all their energy in a tiny volume of living tissue, causing intense ionisation. Outside the body they are stopped by clothing, paper or the outer layer of skin.
Which material is most effective at reducing the intensity of gamma radiation?
A thin sheet of aluminium foil
Gamma rays are highly penetrating and need dense material such as thick lead or concrete to attenuate them. Paper and thin aluminium would block alpha and some beta, but barely affect gamma.
When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, its neutron number
An alpha particle carries away 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so N falls by 2 as well as Z. The mass number falls by 4, which is not the same as the neutron number.
During beta-minus decay, the change inside the nucleus is that
a neutron changes into a proton
a proton changes into a neutron
two protons and two neutrons are ejected
a neutron is ejected from the nucleus
A neutron converts into a proton, an electron (the beta particle) and an antineutrino. The reverse change, proton to neutron, occurs in beta-plus decay.
Gamma radiation is often emitted immediately after an alpha or beta decay because
the nucleus has gained extra protons
the daughter nucleus is left in an excited state
the atom has too many electrons
the alpha or beta particle has been absorbed
The daughter nucleus is often formed in an excited energy state and releases the excess energy as a gamma photon. This changes the energy of the nucleus but not its number of protons or neutrons.
Alpha particles are more strongly ionising than beta particles mainly because they
have a larger charge and move more slowly
Their +2e charge and much greater mass mean they interact strongly with atoms and give up energy over a very short path. A beta particle is lighter and faster, so it is less ionising.
A factory monitors the thickness of paper as it is rolled by placing a radioactive source on one side and a detector on the other. The most suitable source is
an alpha emitter, because it is the most ionising
a gamma emitter, because it is the most penetrating
a source with a very long half-life only
a beta emitter, because the count rate changes with small changes in thickness
Beta particles are partly absorbed by paper, so the detected count varies as the thickness varies. Alpha would be fully stopped and gamma would pass almost unaffected, giving no useful signal.
Thorium-232 (Z = 90) undergoes one alpha decay followed by two beta-minus decays. The final nucleus has
The alpha decay gives A = 228, Z = 88, and each β⁻ decay then raises Z by 1 without changing A, ending at Z = 90. The beta decays do not alter the mass number.
The antineutrino is included in the equation for beta-minus decay because
it carries away the proton's charge
it allows energy and momentum to be conserved
it is needed to balance the mass number
it is the particle that changes into a proton

Beta particles are emitted with a range of energies, so a third particle must share the available energy and momentum. The antineutrino has no charge and almost no mass, so it does not affect A or Z balance.
An electric field is applied between a positive plate and a negative plate while alpha particles pass between them. The alpha particles are deflected
in a circle around the nucleus
Alpha particles carry positive charge, so they are attracted to the negative plate. Beta-minus particles would be deflected the other way, toward the positive plate.
Describe how a sheet of paper, a sheet of aluminium and a block of lead, together with a radiation detector, could be used to identify whether a source emits alpha, beta or gamma radiation. (3 marks)

Measure the count rate with no absorber and subtract background radiation [1] place each absorber in turn between source and detector; a drop with paper indicates alpha, a drop with aluminium indicates beta [1] a count that remains until thick lead is added indicates gamma [1]
Explain why alpha radiation is highly ionising but has low penetrating power, whereas gamma radiation is weakly ionising but highly penetrating. (3 marks)

Alpha particles are massive, slow and carry a +2 charge, so they interact strongly with atoms and strip electrons from them [1] this means they lose their energy in a very short distance and are stopped by paper or a few cm of air [1] gamma photons are uncharged and interact rarely with matter, so they ionise little per unit distance but travel far through dense materials [1]
Radon-222 (Z = 86) decays to polonium (Z = 84) by emitting an alpha particle. Write the nuclear equation. (1 mark)
²²²₈₆Rn → ²¹⁸₈₄Po + ⁴₂He with mass numbers and atomic numbers balanced [1]
A narrow beam containing alpha, beta-minus and gamma radiation passes through a uniform magnetic field. Describe how each type of radiation behaves. (3 marks)

Alpha particles are positively charged and are deflected in one direction along a curved path [1] beta-minus particles are negatively charged and are deflected in the opposite direction, with a tighter curve because of their much smaller mass [1] gamma rays have no charge so they are not deflected [1]

Bismuth-214 (Z = 83) undergoes beta-minus decay to polonium, and the polonium nucleus then undergoes alpha decay to lead. Write the nuclear equation for each decay, identifying the daughter nuclei. (4 marks)

²¹⁴₈₃Bi → ²¹⁴₈₄Po + ⁰₋₁e + antineutrino (ν̄) [1] polonium-214 with Z = 84 identified as the daughter [1] ²¹⁴₈₄Po → ²¹⁰₈₂Pb + ⁴₂He [1] lead-210 with Z = 82 identified, with A and Z balanced in both equations [1]
Thorium-234 (Z = 90) undergoes beta-minus decay. The product nucleus is:
In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted: A stays 234, Z rises by 1.
vce-physics12-half-life-and-activity: physics12a2-hla-1
A sample of a radioisotope contains 80 g of the isotope. The half-life is 6.0 hours. How much of the isotope remains after 24 hours?
24 h is 4 half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5.0 g. Using 2 half-lives (20 g) or 3 (10 g) means mis-counting the number of halvings.
physics12a2-hla-2
The half-life of a radioisotope is best defined as the time taken for
all the nuclei in a sample to decay
half of the nuclei in a sample to decay
a single nucleus to have a 50% chance of decaying twice
the mass of the sample to halve because it loses half its protons
Half-life is the time for half of the radioactive nuclei present to decay, or equivalently for the activity to halve. It is not the time for everything to decay.
physics12a2-hla-3
The activity of a sample falls from 1200 Bq to 150 Bq in 15 days. The half-life is
7.5 days
15 days
2.5 days
5.0 days
physics12a2-hla-4
An activity of 1 becquerel (Bq) means
1 nucleus decays per second
1 joule of radiation energy is absorbed per kilogram
1 nucleus decays per day
1 gram of the material decays per second
The becquerel is one decay per second. Joules per kilogram describes the gray, which measures absorbed dose, not activity.
physics12a2-hla-5
Which statement about radioactive decay of a large sample of identical nuclei is correct?
Heating the sample shortens the half-life
Each nucleus decays exactly once each half-life
It is impossible to predict when any one nucleus will decay, but the fraction decaying in a given time is predictable
Nuclei that have survived longest are most likely to decay next

Decay is random for each nucleus, but with many nuclei the decay rate follows a predictable exponential pattern with a fixed half-life. Half-life is not changed by temperature or by how long a nucleus has already survived.
physics12a2-hla-6
A hospital sample of iodine-131 (half-life 8.0 days) has an initial activity of 64 MBq. Calculate (a) the activity after 24 days and (b) the time for the activity to fall to 2.0 MBq. (3 marks)
(a) 24 days is 3 half-lives: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8.0 MBq; (b) 64 to 2.0 MBq is a factor of 32 = 2⁵, so 5 half-lives; 5 × 8.0 = 40 days.
physics12a2-hla-7
A wooden artefact has a carbon-14 activity of 25% of that of living wood. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years. Estimate the age of the artefact and state one assumption made. (3 marks)

25% is two halvings (100 → 50 → 25), so 2 half-lives; age ≈ 2 × 5730 = 11 460 years (about 1.1 × 10⁴ years); assumption: the ratio of carbon-14 in living organisms (atmosphere) was constant over time, so the original activity equals that of living wood.
physics12a2-hla-8

Technetium-99m (half-life 6.0 hours) is used as a medical tracer. (a) What fraction of the initial activity remains after 24 hours? (b) Explain why a half-life of this length is suitable for a diagnostic tracer. (3 marks)

(a) 24 h is 4 half-lives, (1/2)⁴ = 1/16 ≈ 6.25%; (b) long enough for the imaging to be carried out after preparation and delivery; short enough that the activity (and the patient's dose) falls quickly so it does not stay in the body for long.
vce-physics12-hl-c1
The activity of a sample falls from 800 Bq to 50 Bq in 24 hours. Its half-life is:
3 hours
6 hours
8 hours
12 hours
800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 is 4 half-lives in 24 hours, so the half-life is 6 hours.
vce-physics12-nuclear-fission-and-fusion: physics12a2-nff-1
Which statement best describes nuclear fission?
A neutron changes into a proton inside a nucleus
Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus
A heavy nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, usually after absorbing a neutron
A nucleus emits an alpha particle spontaneously
Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 into two medium-sized fragments plus neutrons, releasing energy. Joining light nuclei is fusion.
physics12a2-nff-2
Nuclear fusion of hydrogen isotopes in a reactor needs extremely high temperatures because
the neutrons must be slowed to thermal speeds
the fuel must be melted before it can react
gamma rays are needed to split the nuclei first
the nuclei must have enough kinetic energy to overcome their electrostatic repulsion and get close enough for the strong force to act
Positively charged nuclei repel each other, so they must collide at very high speeds (temperatures of millions of kelvin) to approach within about 1 fm where the strong nuclear force takes over.
physics12a2-nff-3
Energy is released in both fission of uranium-235 and fusion of hydrogen-2 and hydrogen-3 because
the products have a greater total mass than the reactants
the products have a smaller binding energy per nucleon than the reactants
the products have a greater binding energy per nucleon than the reactants
the number of nucleons decreases

In each case the nuclei move towards the peak of the binding energy curve. The products are more tightly bound, so total mass falls (a mass defect) and the difference appears as energy. The number of nucleons is conserved.
physics12a2-nff-4
The role of control rods in a fission reactor is to
slow neutrons so they can cause fission
absorb neutrons to regulate the rate of the chain reaction
transfer thermal energy to the turbines
supply neutrons to start the reaction
Control rods (for example boron or cadmium) absorb neutrons. Moving them in or out changes how many neutrons go on to cause fission. Slowing neutrons is the role of the moderator.
physics12a2-nff-5
A fission reactor is operating at a steady power output. On average, how many neutrons released by each fission go on to cause another fission?
None
More than three
Exactly one
Two to three

Each fission releases two or three neutrons, but in steady operation the average number that go on to cause another fission is exactly one. More than one gives an accelerating chain reaction; less than one lets it die away.
physics12a2-nff-6
In one fission of a uranium-235 nucleus the total mass decreases by 0.20 u. (1 u = 931.5 MeV; 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.) Calculate the energy released (a) in MeV and (b) in joules. (3 marks)
physics12a2-nff-7
Compare nuclear fission and nuclear fusion in terms of the nuclei involved, the conditions required and the waste produced. (3 marks)

Fission: heavy nuclei (e.g. U-235) split, started by neutron absorption, at moderate temperatures, producing radioactive fission products that need long-term storage; fusion: light nuclei (e.g. H-2 and H-3) join, requiring extremely high temperature and pressure, producing helium and neutrons with much less long-lived waste; both release energy because binding energy per nucleon increases.
physics12a2-nff-8
Explain how a chain reaction is sustained in a fission reactor, and how it is kept under control. (3 marks)

A neutron is absorbed by a U-235 nucleus, which splits and releases two or three more neutrons; these can cause further fissions (a chain reaction); a moderator slows the neutrons so they are more likely to be absorbed; control rods absorb excess neutrons so that, on average, one neutron per fission causes another fission and the power stays steady.
vce-physics12-nf-c1
In one fission reaction, the mass of the products is 3.1 × 10⁻²⁸ kg less than the mass of the reactants. How much energy is released?
About 2.8 × 10⁻¹¹ J
E = mc² = 3.1 × 10⁻²⁸ × (3.0 × 10⁸)² ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻¹¹ J. The missing mass (mass defect) is converted to energy.
vce-physics12-radiation-dose-and-biologi: The gray (Gy), the unit of absorbed dose, is equivalent to
Absorbed dose is energy absorbed per unit mass, so 1 Gy = 1 J kg⁻¹. One decay per second is the becquerel; one joule per coulomb is the volt.
A patient's tissue of mass 5.0 kg absorbs 0.40 J of radiation energy. The absorbed dose is
D = E/m = 0.40 / 5.0 = 0.080 Gy. 12.5 Gy is the result of inverting the ratio (5.0 / 0.40).
For the same absorbed dose, alpha radiation causes more biological damage than gamma radiation when absorbed inside the body mainly because alpha particles
deposit their energy over a very short path, producing dense ionisation

Alpha particles are heavily ionising, depositing all their energy in a tiny volume of tissue, so they cause concentrated damage. This is reflected in their larger radiation weighting factor when equivalent dose is calculated.
A technician stands 1.0 m from a small gamma source and measures a dose rate of 40 µSv h⁻¹. Treating the source as a point source, the dose rate at 2.0 m would be

Intensity from a point source follows an inverse-square law. Doubling the distance reduces the dose rate to one quarter: 40 / 4 = 10 µSv h⁻¹. 20 µSv h⁻¹ would result from an inverse (not inverse-square) relationship.
Which of the following is a long-term (chronic) effect of exposure to ionising radiation?
An increased risk of cancer years later
Nausea and vomiting within a day
Damage to DNA that is not repaired can lead to cancer many years later, with the probability rising with the total dose received. Burns, nausea and sickness are acute effects of high doses.

A worker's tissue of mass 50 kg absorbs 2.5 mJ of energy from alpha particles. (a) Calculate the absorbed dose. (b) The radiation weighting factor for alpha radiation is 20. Calculate the equivalent dose. (3 marks)

A gamma source gives a dose rate of 80 µSv h⁻¹ at a distance of 1.0 m. (a) State the three main ways of reducing exposure to a radiation source. (b) Calculate the dose received by a person who works 3.0 hours at a distance of 2.0 m (assume a point source and no shielding). (3 marks)
(a) reduce the time of exposure, increase the distance, use shielding (e.g. lead); (b) at 2.0 m the dose rate is 80 / 2² = 20 µSv h⁻¹; dose = 20 × 3.0 = 60 µSv.
Explain how ionising radiation can damage living cells, and why radiotherapy is able to destroy tumours. (3 marks)

Ionising radiation removes electrons from atoms and molecules in cells, producing ions and free radicals that can break DNA strands or alter bases; damaged cells may die, mutate or become cancerous if the damage is not repaired; rapidly dividing cells (such as tumour cells) are more sensitive; radiotherapy aims a high dose at the tumour from several directions to kill cancer cells while limiting the dose to surrounding healthy tissue.
Tissue absorbs a dose of 2.0 mGy of alpha radiation (radiation weighting factor 20). The equivalent dose is:
Equivalent dose = absorbed dose × weighting factor = 2.0 × 20 = 40 mSv. Alpha particles are highly ionising inside the body.
vce-physics12-charge-current-and-potenti: A current of 3.0 A flows through a heater for 20 s. How much charge passes through the heater?
Q = I t = 3.0 × 20 = 60 C. Dividing (20 / 3.0 = 6.7) is the wrong operation.
A 12 V battery moves 5.0 C of charge around a circuit. The total energy transferred to the circuit is
The potential difference is energy per unit charge, so W = qV = 5.0 × 12 = 60 J.
In a simple circuit with a cell and a lamp, conventional current flows
from the negative terminal to the positive terminal outside the cell
from the positive terminal to the negative terminal outside the cell
in the same direction as the electron flow
By convention, current is defined as the flow of positive charge, from the positive terminal through the external circuit to the negative terminal. The electrons move in the opposite direction.
A charge of 4.8 C passes a point in a wire. The charge on one electron is 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. How many electrons passed the point?
To measure the current through a lamp and the potential difference across it, the meters should be connected so that
the ammeter is in parallel with the lamp and the voltmeter is in series with it
both meters are in parallel with the lamp
the ammeter is in series with the lamp and the voltmeter is in parallel with it
both meters are in series with the lamp

The ammeter has very low resistance and must carry the lamp's current, so it goes in series. The voltmeter has very high resistance and measures the difference between two points, so it goes in parallel.

A current of 0.25 A flows in a circuit for 2.0 minutes. (a) Calculate the charge that passes. (b) Calculate the number of electrons that this charge represents (e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). (c) If the supply is 6.0 V, calculate the energy transferred. (3 marks)
Distinguish between electric current and potential difference in a circuit. (3 marks)

Current is the rate of flow of charge past a point (I = Q/t), measured in amperes and measured in series with a component; potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points (V = W/q), measured in volts and measured in parallel across a component; current is a flow through the component while potential difference is across it (the supply provides the energy, charge carriers do not get used up).
A lamp passes 90 C of charge in 5.0 minutes while transferring 540 J of electrical energy. Calculate (a) the current in the lamp, (b) the potential difference across it and (c) its power. (3 marks)
A current of 2.0 A flows for 3.0 minutes. How much charge passes, and how many electrons is that?
Q = It = 2.0 × 180 = 360 C. Number of electrons = 360 ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 2.25 × 10²¹. Convert minutes to seconds.
vce-physics12-resistance-and-ohms-law: physics12a2-rol-1
A resistor has a potential difference of 9.0 V across it and a current of 0.30 A through it. Its resistance is
R = V / I = 9.0 / 0.30 = 30 Ω. 2.7 comes from multiplying V by I, which gives power.
physics12a2-rol-2
A metal wire has resistance R. A second wire of the same material has twice the length and twice the diameter. Its resistance is
2R
4R
R
R is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Twice the length gives ×2; twice the diameter gives four times the area, so ×1/4. Net factor is 2/4 = 1/2, giving R/2.
physics12a2-rol-3
An ohmic conductor at constant temperature has a current-potential difference graph that is
a curve that gets steeper as the potential difference increases
a curve that flattens as the potential difference increases
a straight line through the origin
a horizontal straight line
For an ohmic conductor I is proportional to V, so the I–V graph is a straight line through the origin; the gradient is 1/R. Curves are typical of non-ohmic devices.
physics12a2-rol-4
As the current through the filament of a lamp increases, its resistance increases. This is mainly because
the potential difference across the filament decreases
the filament gets shorter
the number of charge carriers decreases
the higher temperature causes more frequent collisions between charge carriers and the vibrating lattice
A larger current heats the filament, increasing lattice vibrations, so conduction electrons collide more often and the resistance rises. The filament is therefore non-ohmic.
physics12a2-rol-5
A 4.0 Ω heating element is connected to a 12 V supply. The power dissipated is
P = V²/R = 12² / 4.0 = 36 W (check: I = 3.0 A, P = VI = 36 W). 48 W comes from V × R.
physics12a2-rol-6

A length of uniform wire of length 1.5 m has a resistance of 6.0 Ω. A second wire of the same material has a length of 4.5 m and half the diameter. (a) Calculate the resistance of the second wire. (b) State the relationships you used. (3 marks)

(a) length ×3 gives ×3; half the diameter gives one quarter the area, so resistance ×4; R = 6.0 × 3 × 4 = 72 Ω; (b) R is directly proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (area proportional to diameter squared) for the same material.
physics12a2-rol-7

A student measures the following for a component: 1.0 V, 0.10 A; 2.0 V, 0.18 A; 3.0 V, 0.24 A. (a) Calculate the resistance at each point. (b) State whether the component is ohmic and justify your answer. (3 marks)

(a) R = V/I gives 10 Ω, 11 Ω (11.1), 12.5 Ω; (b) the component is non-ohmic because its resistance is not constant (I is not proportional to V; the I–V graph curves rather than being a straight line through the origin); resistance increases as current increases, consistent with heating.
physics12a2-rol-8
An electric heater is rated at 230 V and draws a current of 8.0 A. Calculate (a) its resistance, (b) its power, and (c) the energy it transfers in 30 minutes, in joules. (3 marks)
vce-physics12-ro-c1
The I–V graph of a filament lamp curves so that current increases less and less as voltage rises. This shows that:
The lamp is non-ohmic: its resistance decreases as the filament heats up
The lamp obeys Ohm's law, because current always rises with voltage
The current is independent of voltage once the filament is glowing
The lamp is non-ohmic: its resistance increases as the filament heats up
R = V/I rises along the curve. Hotter metal has more vibrating ions, which impede electron flow.
vce-physics12-series-and-parallel-circui: A 10 Ω resistor and a 20 Ω resistor are connected in series to a 12 V supply. The current in the circuit is
R total = 10 + 20 = 30 Ω; I = V/R = 12 / 30 = 0.40 A. 0.60 A would result from using only the 20 Ω resistor.
A 6.0 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is
1/R = 1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12, so R = 4.0 Ω. The equivalent resistance of a parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor.
Two identical lamps are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply. The potential difference across each lamp is
Branches of a parallel circuit are connected across the same two points, so each has the full supply potential difference of 12 V. In series, the supply voltage would be shared.
One lamp burns out (becomes an open circuit) in a circuit with three lamps. All three lamps go out. The lamps must have been connected
in a mix of series and parallel with the burnt lamp in a branch
